articles.title: EU moves to ban tankers insured in Russia, repair services at Russian refineries
articles.summary: The EU has moved to ban all tankers insured in Russia and bar European companies from helping build, operate or repair Russian energy infrastructure, including refineries, in a new sanctions package that may further disrupt Russian crude and refined products trade flows. European Commission President Ursula von der...
articles.body: EU moves to ban tankers insured in Russia, repair services at Russian refineries in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 The EU has moved to ban all tankers insured in Russia and bar European companies from helping build, operate or repair Russian energy infrastructure, including refineries, in a new sanctions package that may further disrupt Russian crude and refined products trade flows. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the measures on Nov. 23, which also include the first-ever EU ban on Russian “electricity services” and the addition of more than 70 vessels to the bloc’s shadow fleet designation list. “The aim is to keep pressure on Russia to end their war of aggression in Ukraine. And we will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia shows genuine intent for a lasting peace in Ukraine,” von der Leyen said in a statement published on the Commission website. No further details on the tanker ban are available. EU ports generally accept ships covered by the International Group of P&I Clubs, and an analysis of S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) and Maritime Intelligence Risk Suite data finds no oil and chemical tankers that have so far in November discharged cargoes in the Netherlands — where Europe’s top cargo port, Rotterdam, is located — are covered by Russian insurance firms. Brussels has previously sanctioned several Russian marine insurers, including Russian National Reinsurance Co, while banning EU-based companies from insuring ships involved in Russian oil trades unless the barrels were sold at below certain thresholds under the price cap system. For the 22nd package of sanctions against Russia to be adopted, all 27 EU member states must approve it. Unanimous agreement on EU sanctions has previously proved difficult to secure, with some member states historically seeking carve-outs or delaying consensus. In July, the EU sanctioned a string of additional refineries under its 21st package of sanctions against Russia, including Belarus’s Mozyr, Georgia’s Kulevi and three Russian facilities. The bloc previously banned direct seaborne imports of Russia’s crude and fuel in 2022-23. In January 2026, the EU introduced a new ban on products made from Russian oil in third countries. Additionally, it listed specific refiners in India and China. “The 22nd package looks like it mainly targets the financial sector,” Tanya Stepanova, head of Eurasia and Africa refining coverage for S&P Global Energy CERA, said. “European refining technology and service providers were once deeply embedded in Russia’s refining sector,” Stepanova added. “The majority of Russia’s secondary processing units were built on foreign technology, European and American. Yet European firms withdrew from the market almost immediately after the war began [in 2022]. For that reason, I do not expect the immediate impact of this sanction package to be material.” Source: Platts 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: One in Five Newbuilding Orders This Year Belong to Greek Interests
articles.summary: Greek owners have been accumulating newbuilding orders so far this year, as prices keep grinding higher. articles.body: One in Five Newbuilding Orders This Year Belong to Greek Interests in Hellenic Shipping News 25/11/2026 G reek owners have been accumulating newbuilding orders so far this year, as prices keep grinding higher. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “Greek owners account for more than one in five newbuilding orders placed in 2026 across bulk carriers, tankers, containerships and gas carriers, with 455 contracts out of 2,200 worldwide. Their participation in this year’s contracting exceeds their share of the outstanding orderbook across the three main conventional sectors. Greeks represent 16.4% of new bulker orders against 11.3% of the global bulker orderbook, 30.7% against 27.0% in tankers, and 14.5% against 12.6% in containers. These figures underline the substantial Greek contribution to the next generation of shipping capacity”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker According to Xclusiv, “almost half of the Greek dry bulk orderbook reflects contracts placed this year. The 100 vessels ordered in 2026 are equivalent to 48.3% of the 207 ships outstanding, compared with 33.3% globally. The preference for larger tonnage is pronounced. Capesizes and Newcastlemaxes account for 45% of Greek bulker contracts, against 24% worldwide. Furthermore, 22 of the 25 Newcastlemaxes on the Greek orderbook were contracted this year, while Greek owners placed 23 of the 32 Capesize orders recorded globally. This concentration gives Greek investment decisions particular significance for future competition in the larger sizes. The supply implications vary considerably within dry bulk. The global orderbook has reached 15.7% of fleet dwt, from 10.7% a year earlier. However, the combined Cape/VLOC orderbook by vessel count is equivalent to 282% of the fleet aged 21 years and above, compared with 62% for Handysizes. Larger bulkers consequently have greater potential for fleet expansion beyond replacement of the oldest ships. Handysize supply commitments remain more restrained, although Greek participation in this year’s ordering is limited to one vessel out of 73 worldwide”. Meanwhile, “tankers attracted 211 Greek contracts, accounting for 46% of Greek ordering across the four sectors and equivalent to 46.1% of the outstanding Greek tanker orderbook. VLCCs and Suezmaxes dominate with 68 and 50 orders respectively, together representing 56% of Greek tanker contracts. Greeks account for approximately half of worldwide Suezmax ordering and 39% of VLCC/ULCC contracting this year. Their investment therefore carries substantial exposure to the future balance of large crude tanker markets. Fleet ageing provides a basis for tanker renewal, with approximately 48% of vessels aged 16 years or above. Meanwhile, the global orderbook has increased to 26.1% of fleet dwt, from 15.3% a year earlier. Delivery schedules place much of this capacity further ahead. Approximately 76% of VLCC/ULCC and 73% of Suezmax ordered dwt is scheduled for 2028 onwards. The commercial effect will depend partly on how much older capacity leaves service before these deliveries arrive”, Xclusiv said. The shipbroker added that “containerships present another distinct replacement profile. Greek owners placed 99 orders this year, equivalent to 39.9% of their outstanding programme, concentrating on Feeders, Handies and Panamaxes. Globally, the orderbook stands at 44.5% of fleet TEU capacity, up from 32% a year earlier. Yet the 642 Feeders on order represent only 54% of the 1,184 existing vessels aged 21 or above. This provides considerable potential for replacement within a sector facing substantial overall capacity additions”. Finally, “gas investment adds further exposure to expanding delivery pipelines, with 45 Greek contracts, including 25 VLGCs and 16 LNG carriers of 141,000–200,000 cbm. The global VLGC orderbook already represents 48.3% of fleet capacity, while LNG stands at 36.5%. Across these investment programmes, earnings will influence both owners’ willingness to retire older vessels and the market’s ability to absorb deliveries”, Xclusiv concluded. Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide Tops 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Good Times Bad Times: The Premium Stays with the Strait
articles.summary: In October, we wrote that if the transfer network off Oman kept pace, Gulf crude would carry China’s refill and keep drawing tonnage east, supporting earnings on both routes. The relay largely kept pace. The earnings split: freight outside the Strait gave back most of its gains, while freight inside it held on. The...
articles.body: Good Times Bad Times: The Premium Stays with the Strait in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 I n October, we wrote that if the transfer network off Oman kept pace, Gulf crude would carry China’s refill and keep drawing tonnage east, supporting earnings on both routes. The relay largely kept pace. The earnings split: freight outside the Strait gave back most of its gains, while freight inside it held on. The cost of chartering a VLCC from the Gulf of Oman to China (TD34) reached 841 Worldscale on 8 October, the highest level since the route began to be assessed in March. By 20 November it stood at 328, down 61%. Over the same six weeks the run loading inside the Strait of Hormuz (TD3C) fell by 22% (Figure 1). The obvious reading is that cargo abandoned loading outside the Strait and went back inside. Port and fixture data do not support it. The explanation is simpler. Freight outside the Strait fell with the rest of the VLCC market, and freight inside it did not, because it carries a premium for the transit itself. Figure 1: VLCC freight to China from the day the Gulf of Oman assessment peaked, Worldscale indexed to 8 October 2026 = 100. TD3C Middle East Gulf to China and TD34 Gulf of Oman to China, both 270,000 tonnes, weekdays only. Source: Baltic Exchange. Over the same six weeks, in Worldscale terms (lump sum for TD22), West Africa to China (TD15) fell by 60% and the US Gulf to China run (TD22) by 56%, both well away from the Gulf. The dividing line is not the length of the voyage, since the long haul Gulf to China run (TD3C) barely moved. It is the Hormuz transit. Of the four VLCC routes into China, only the one that crosses the Strait held most of its value, and the Gulf of Oman route fell with the routes from West Africa and the US Gulf. The premium stayed with the Strait TD3C runs from Ras Tanura to Ningbo, about 10% further than TD34 from Mina Al Fahal. Yet on 8 October TD3C was assessed at 1.6 times TD34 in Worldscale points, and on 20 November at 3.1 times. Both routes are priced off fixed annual flat rates, so the gap in dollars moved the same way. Base freight fell everywhere, and the price of the transit itself widened. Saudi Aramco’s pricing points the same way. It set the November Arab Light price to Asia at US$ 5.00 below the Oman and Dubai average, a cut of US$ 3.00, to compensate buyers for freight, and has reportedly widened the discount again for December. The seller is absorbing part of the transit cost rather than expecting it to disappear. Tonnage tightened, then recovered Figure 2: The Gulf tonnage pool, unsanctioned VLCCs, spot and contract, able to reach the Arabian Gulf within 30 days of opening, against the Gulf of Oman assessment (TD34). The lower panel tests the relationship at a nineteen trading day lag. Source: Signal Ocean (route supply, TD3C basis), Baltic Exchange. Figure 2 shows the Gulf tonnage pool: unsanctioned VLCCs, on spot and on contract, that could reach the Arabian Gulf within 30 days of their next open date. It is a wider measure than the net supply count. A ship discharging in China enters the count as soon as its open date and position qualify, so about half of the latest count is still laden or discharging in the Far East. The lower panel asks whether a change in that count predicts the next move in freight. For each date it plots the percentage change in available VLCCs over the previous nineteen trading days against the percentage change in the Gulf of Oman assessment over the following nineteen. If tonnage leads freight, the points should slope downwards: fewer ships first, higher rates after. Measured on every trading day, consecutive windows would share eighteen of their nineteen days, so the panel also uses blocks nineteen days apart that do not overlap, which leaves seven independent observations over the life of the route. The Gulf tonnage pool hit its lowest level of the year on 19 September and touched it again on 23 September. By late November it was back around its 2026 average. The Gulf of Oman assessment climbed from about 260 Worldscale on 1 September to about 800 by 17 September, reaching that level in the same days that the pool fell to its trough. It then held between roughly 750 and 840 for three weeks while the pool recovered by about a quarter. The relationship cannot generalise. The Gulf of Oman route has been assessed for 167 trading days, which at a nineteen day horizon leaves seven independent observations, and on those the correlation of −0.34 is not distinguishable from noise. The sign is negative whichever day the blocks start on, so the September episode is consistent with tonnage mattering, but seven points cannot turn it into a rule. The relay through Fujairah kept running Figure 3: Fully fixed VLCC fixtures per calendar day by reported load port, with Fujairah as a share of the region. Ship-to-ship cargoes are reported as loading at Fujairah, and Fujairah includes pipeline loadings at the ADCOP single buoy mooring. Inside the Strait: Ras Tanura, Basrah, Kuwait. November covers 1 to 20 November. Source: Signal Ocean. Over the past 60 days, 77% of VLCC loading calls at Fujairah were at the anchorage, where cargo is transferred from other vessels, and 21% at the ADCOP single buoy mooring, which loads crude piped from Abu Dhabi. Where the delivering vessel can be identified, it is almost always another VLCC shuttling cargo out through the Strait. That relay did not stop. VLCC fixtures loading at Fujairah ran at 2.9 a day in September, 2.1 in October and 2.5 in the first twenty days of November, against 0.2 to 0.5 a day loading inside the Strait (Figure 3). Fujairah’s share of fixtures in the region was 85% in September and 74% in both October and November. The relay eased only slightly. Our AIS tracking counts 20 to 24 VLCC transfer loadings a week at Fujairah and Sohar from late August to mid October, with one week at 32, and 16 to 21 a week from late October, while fixtures and cargo counts out of the region held steady. Waits shortened too, the median time from arrival to loaded falling from 190 hours in September to 138 hours in November. Figure 4: The Gulf tonnage pool, unsanctioned VLCCs, spot and contract, able to reach the Arabian Gulf within 30 days of opening, and TD34 Gulf of Oman to China, from 26 March, when TD34 was first assessed, to 23 and 20 November respectively. Each is rebased to its own average over that period = 100 (274.3 vessels, 323 Worldscale) on its own axis, so both averages sit on the dashed line. Shading marks supply above (blue) or below (red) its average and TD34 above its average (grey). Source: Signal Ocean (route supply, TD3C basis), Baltic Exchange. The squeeze on ships came when the pool was at its thinnest. The Gulf tonnage pool fell to its 2026 low on 19 September, a quarter below its average since March. In the same weeks TD34 rose to about two and a half times its own average (Figure 4). As the relay sped up it released about ten VLCCs, from roughly 28 tied up in September to 18 from October, and by 23 November the pool was back around its average, with TD34 back on its average too. That helped end the September squeeze, but it is too small to account on its own for a 61% fall that matched routes with no exposure to the Gulf. The squeeze that came and went The disruption premium has not gone. It has concentrated on the Strait itself. The Gulf tonnage pool is back around its average (Figure 4) and freight outside the Strait has fallen back with the wider market, while the premium for the transit was wider on 20 November than on 8 October. Arabian Gulf–China loadings are broadly unchanged from October. The focus is now on whether incoming ballasters, meet sufficient fresh cargo demand. Source: By Nikolas Zannikos, Signal Group, https://www.thesignalgroup.com/newsroom/market-insights-good-times-bad-times-the-premium-stays-with-the-strait Tops 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The earnings split: freight outside the Strait gave back most of its gains, while freight inside it held on.
The cost of chartering a VLCC from the Gulf of Oman to China (TD34) reached 841 Worldscale on 8 October, the highest level since the route began to be assessed in March.
By 20 November it stood at 328, down 61%.

articles.title: China is back buying US soybeans at harvest, as US wheat exports fall by about a third
articles.summary: China took about 4.3 Mt of US soybeans in September and October, against almost none a year earlier during the trade war. Our view is that US soybean shipments to China look to be heading about 15% higher over the July to June 2026/27 season, with more of the buying at harvest time and less ...
articles.body: China is back buying US soybeans at harvest, as US wheat exports fall by about a third in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 25/11/2026 China took about 4.3 Mt of US soybeans in September and October, against almost none a year earlier during the trade war. Our view is that US soybean shipments to China look to be heading about 15% higher over the July to June 2026/27 season, with more of the buying at harvest time and less in the spring. US wheat moves the other way. Exports in July to October were about 39% lower than a year earlier, and we expect them to be about 30% lower over the season. That reflects drought in the US Plains rather than tariffs. For ships, it means more US Panamax cargoes going to China this winter and less Supramax demand from the US Gulf over the season. US soybeans to China, back at harvest Last season, China bought almost no US new-crop soybeans until the Busan truce in late October 2025, then bought heavily from December to March. This season the buying has returned to its usual timing. US bean shipments to China were about 2.1 Mt in September and 2.2 Mt in October, and we expect around 4.2 Mt in October to December, almost three times last year. The tariff gap remains. China kept a 10% retaliatory tariff on US beans, so they pay about 13% duty against 3% for Brazilian beans, and the truce now runs to 10 January 2027. From January we expect US shipments to China to be below last season’s post-truce catch-up, at around 5.2 Mt in January to March against 7.8 Mt. Over the season, we expect about 14 Mt, still well below the 25 Mt a year the US says China agreed to buy. Source: Tradeviews research. US soybean shipments to China and US wheat exports by quarter, July to June seasons. Recent months are Tradeviews estimates and may be revised; forecast from November. US wheat exports fall US wheat exports in July to October were about 5.5 Mt, against 9.0 Mt a year earlier. This is not a tariff story, as China takes very little US wheat. Drought across the Southern Plains cut the hard red winter crop, and in August the USDA put US wheat production about 26% lower and exports nearly 15% lower this season. High fertiliser costs added to the pressure. Weekly US wheat shipments in late October were the lowest since records began in 1983. It is part of a wider squeeze. The USDA expects wheat production among the seven largest exporters to fall by about 11% this season, with Canada, Australia, Argentina and the EU all lower, while Russian and Ukrainian supplies face shipping disruption. We expect US wheat exports to stay below last season through to May, and to be about 30% lower over the season. Total US grain exports look to be about 6% lower, with maize close to last season through the winter and about 13% higher from April to June. The rest of the season Elsewhere, Brazilian soybean exports look to show a small rise, with the new crop loading from February. Brazilian maize exports were almost 30% lower in July to October, and we expect November to February to be close to last season. Argentine soybean and meal exports look about 28% lower over the season, and Canadian grain exports about 11% higher. The war in Ukraine continues to weigh on Black Sea trade. Ukraine reportedly exported 1.26 Mt of grains and pulses in October, down nearly 50% on a year earlier, with wheat making up 954,000 t. We expect Ukrainian loadings to stay well below last season to December, before the maize harvest lifts them from January. Russia is having difficulty getting grain to alternative ports, and we expect Russian grain loadings in January to March to be around 40% below last season, then recovering from April. Source: Tradeviews research. Main loading months by crop, July to June. Bars before “Now” compare the season so far with last season; lighter bars are our forecast. What it means for ships We measure ship demand in agribulk tonne-days, which count the ballast leg as well as the laden voyage, so long hauls such as the US Gulf to China count for more than short ones. For Panamaxes, the change is mainly in where US cargoes go rather than how many there are. US Panamax agricultural exports in October to December look to be about 5% higher than a year earlier, as soybean cargoes to China roughly double while shipments to other buyers ease. From January, with less catch-up buying from China, US Panamax agricultural exports look to be about 7% lower than last season. Lower wheat exports weigh more on Supramaxes, and we expect US Gulf Supramax demand to be about 12% lower over the season. Across all grain trades, we expect agribulk tonne-days to be about 3% lower for Panamaxes and about 1.5% lower for Supramaxes over the season. Lower Argentine soybean, Brazilian maize and US wheat exports, and fewer Russian cargoes before April, more than offset more Brazilian soybeans. Source: Tradeviews research. Ships employed in the agribulk trade by month, July to June seasons. Reported data, then Tradeviews estimates for recent months, then forecast from November. Where positioning may matter ▪ US Gulf, November and December. More soybean cargoes to China than a year earlier, with maize close to last season. ▪ US Gulf, January to March. Fewer soybean cargoes to China than last season’s post-truce surge. ▪ East Coast South America, March to June. More Brazilian soybean cargoes than last season, but fewer from Argentina. ▪ Black Sea, from April. Our forecast has Russian loadings recovering after a weak January to March. Risks in both directions On the upside, China could buy more US soybeans to move closer to its pledge, and an easing of the war would let Russian and Ukrainian grain move more freely. On the downside, the US and China truce could lapse in January, which would hit US soybean cargoes from the US Gulf and Pacific Northwest. In Brazil, a stronger El Niño could hit the soybean crop that loads from February. The most uncertain call is US soybeans after January. Our forecast assumes China keeps buying at a lower rate than last spring. A renewed tariff dispute could cut that further, while a wider deal could lift it towards the pledged level. Data note Data from Tradeviews research. Volumes cover grain, soybeans and soybean meal from the US, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Australia, Russia, Ukraine and the main EU exporters; shipments to China are by declared next port of call. Agribulk tonne-days cover Panamaxes and Supramaxes, including sugar, and count the ballast leg. Customs data run to August or September 2026 depending on the country; later months are Tradeviews estimates and may be revised; forecast from November 2026. Seasons run July to June. Ships employed assume average cargoes of 85,000 t for Panamaxes and 60,000 t for Supramaxes. Source: By Russell Thompson, CEO of Tradeviews*, https://tradeviews.net/us-soybeans-china-wheat-2026-27/ * Russell Thompson is the Founder and CEO of Tradeviews, which he set up in 2012. Tradeviews forecasts dry bulk and tanker trade flows and freight from country-level customs data, covering trade volumes, tonne-days and ships employed by vessel size. Before Tradeviews, Russell was Head of Research at Gearbulk. More analysis at tradeviews.net. 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Why 200,000m³ LNG carriers could be the next step in fleet renewal
articles.summary: For LNG shipping, the question of vessel size has always involved a careful trade-off. Increasing cargo capacity can improve transport efficiency, but those gains have limited value if a ship becomes too large for the infrastructure it needs to serve. A new technical and commercial assessment of 200,000m³ LNG carrier...
articles.body: Why 200,000m³ LNG carriers could be the next step in fleet renewal in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 F or LNG shipping, the question of vessel size has always involved a careful trade-off. Increasing cargo capacity can improve transport efficiency, but those gains have limited value if a ship becomes too large for the infrastructure it needs to serve. A new technical and commercial assessment of 200,000m³ LNG carrier concepts, produced by LR Advisory for GTT and presented at Gastech 2026, suggests the industry may be approaching a useful middle ground, where vessels are significantly larger than the conventional 174,000m³ LNG carrier, but still capable of accessing much of the existing global terminal network. Constantinos Chaelis, Global Gas Segment Director, LR 200,000 vs 174,000 LR analysis compared representative 200,000m³ designs with a 174,000m³ LNG carrier, examining terminal accessibility alongside representative commercial Atlantic and Pacific operating scenarios. It found that a 200,000m³ vessel could access approximately 88 LNG terminals globally, compared with 97 for its 174,000m³ counterpart. The reduction in accessibility is important, but the geographical distribution of those restrictions matters. Modern terminals in China, South Korea, Singapore and Northern Europe are generally compatible with 200,000m³ LNG carrier operations. Restrictions are more concentrated among older terminals, particularly in Japan. This distinction could prove central to the case for upsizing. Rather than requiring a fundamental rebuilding of the LNG terminal network, a 200,000m³ vessel could potentially operate across many of the trades already central to the global LNG market. “The significance of these findings is that larger LNG carriers do not appear to require a wholesale rethink of terminal infrastructure,” says Constantinos Chaelis, Global Gas Segment Director at LR. “Many key LNG hubs are already capable of supporting these vessel concepts, which gives the market a realistic pathway to improve transport efficiency while maintaining broad trading optionality,” he says. François Michel, Chief Executive Officer, GTT (left) receives LR Advisory’s terminal compatibility and commercial evaluation report for GTT from Andy McKeran, LR’s Chief Growth Officer, at Gastech 2026 The practical limits of scale This assessment considered eight representative 200,000m³ three and four-tank vessel concepts. Overall lengths of these notional ships ranged from 291.4m to 300m and beam from 47m to 51m, with a draught of 11.5m. Interestingly, cargo tank configuration itself did not emerge as the determining factor in terminal accessibility. Based on the vessel particulars and terminal constraints reviewed, the analysis identified no material difference in terminal accessibility between three and four-tank arrangements. The more significant factor was beam. Beam restrictions were the most common limitation, followed by displacement. Draft restrictions were relatively limited, while vessel length proved generally less critical than anticipated. One 51m-beam concept encountered restrictions at terminals with a 50m beam limit, showing how small adjustment to dimensions can materially affect trading flexibility. This creates an important distinction for future design development. Displacement compatibility can sometimes be influenced by the loading condition and cargo density, and therefore assessed during voyage planning and terminal acceptance. A beam restriction is inherently harder to mitigate against without changing the vessel design. “The conclusion is not simply that bigger LNG carriers work, but that careful optimisation of their principal dimensions matters. Capacity needs to be increased without moving the vessel beyond the infrastructure envelope required by its intended trading pattern,” says Chaelis. More cargo at lower speeds The potential case for larger LNG carriers also needs to be viewed against changing operating patterns. The report identifies increasing LNG trade volumes, longer-haul trades, an ageing fleet and a greater focus on efficiency and reducing emissions among the structural factors influencing the market. It also points towards the use of lower operating speeds as the industry seeks greater efficiency. The assessment refers to operating speeds of around 15.3 knots compared with traditional LNG carrier speeds of about 19 knots. As lower speeds reduce the number of voyages that can be completed over a given period, additional transportation capacity may be needed to compensate. A larger vessel means more LNG can be transported on each voyage, potentially reducing the number of sailings required per unit of cargo moved and improving overall transport efficiency. “The industry is entering a period where fleet renewal decisions will shape LNG transportation for decades to come,” says Sujith Tooneri, one of the authors of the detailed feasibility assessment. “Our analysis shows that 200,000m³ LNG carriers can retain access to most major LNG terminals while increasing cargo carrying capacity, making them a practical option for owners looking to improve transportation efficiency and support future trade growth.” The issue is relevant to fleet renewal as the assessment notes an ageing LNG carrier fleet requiring replacement alongside growing LNG trade volumes, strong shipyard orderbooks and demand for more efficient vessel designs. Testing the commercial case Greater capacity must still justify the additional investment. Here, the modelling provides a further argument for considering the 200,000m³ scale. Under the representative scenarios modelled in the study, the assessment indicates approximately US$85 million in additional owner benefit over 30 years, with a net present value of US$78.1 million, an internal rate of return of 8.3% and an estimated payback period of approximately 10 years. The potential benefits for charterers are larger in absolute terms under the assumptions modelled. The study estimates a 30-year benefit of US$1.38 billion for a US-Europe trading scenario under EU regulations and US$1.48 billion for the same trade under the modelled IMO framework. For the longer US-Asia trade, the equivalent modelled benefits are US$680.4 million under the IMO framework and US$804.2 million in the scenario without regulations. These figures should not be read as forecasts of financial performance. The report states that the benefits are based on representative trading scenarios, market assumptions and modelling conducted as part of the study. Actual performance may vary depending on market conditions, vessel design and operational profile. And that caveat is important. So too is the relatively modest difference in the headline terminal-access figures. The commercial assessment moves from 97 accessible terminals for a conventional 174,000m³ carrier to 88 for the larger vessel, while increasing nominal cargo capacity by 26,000m. A question of optimisation, not simply size The case for the 200,000m³ LNG carrier is therefore more nuanced than simply building a larger ship. For the next generation of LNG carriers, the debate may be less about whether the fleet should become larger and more about how far it can scale while retaining sufficient flexibility. “The 200,000m³ concept does not remove every infrastructure constraint, nor will it suit every trade. What the analysis shows is that the step from 174,000m³ to 200,000m³ can be technically feasible across much of the existing terminal network and commercially attractive under the scenarios assessed,” says Tooneri. For an industry preparing to make fleet decisions with implications stretching decades into the future, that changes the discussion. “The question is no longer simply whether LNG carriers can become larger, but whether additional capacity can be designed into the next generation of vessels while preserving the flexibility that has made the modern LNG fleet globally tradable,” concludes Chaelis. articles.title: Open letter to the Members of the European Parliament to reject the motion for a resolution and support the inclusion of Indian ship recycling yards on the European List
articles.summary: Dear Members of the European Parliament, Ahead of this week’s plenary vote, European Shipowners | ECSA, BIMCO, the Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), INTERCARGO, INTERFERRY, INTERTANKO and the World Shipping Council (WSC) call on MEPs to reject the motion for a...
articles.body: Open letter to the Members of the European Parliament to reject the motion for a resolution and support the inclusion of Indian ship recycling yards on the European List in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 Dear Members of the European Parliament, Ahead of this week’s plenary vote, European Shipowners | ECSA, BIMCO, the Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), INTERCARGO, INTERFERRY, INTERTANKO and the World Shipping Council (WSC) call on MEPs to reject the motion for a resolution objecting to the European Commission’s proposal to add two Indian ship recycling facilities to the European List of Ship Recycling Facilities. Follow the evidence, avoid double standards The two Indian yards were thoroughly evaluated during an extensive, independent inspection process and found compliant with the EU Ship Recycling Regulation (EU SRR), as demonstrated by the publicly available inspection reports. They meet the same requirements of the EU SRR and its Technical Guidance Note that have underpinned every previous edition of the European List. Inclusion should be determined solely on whether a facility meets these safety and environmental requirements, based on objective assessments and inspections. Declining to approve facilities that objectively meet the standards the EU has itself agreed would undermine the credibility of the EU’s own legislation. We call on Parliament to base its decision on facts and evidence: non-OECD yards that meet the EU SRR’s requirements can and should be recognised. Reward progress towards safe and environmentally sound ship recycling worldwide The proposed inclusion reflects years of substantial investment and effort since the adoption of the Hong Kong Convention (HKC) in 2009. The yards concerned have made considerable capital investments to upgrade their infrastructure, safety systems and environmental management to meet the HKC and EU SRR standards. These efforts embody the very purpose of the EU SRR: to reduce disparities between operators in the EU, in the OECD and in relevant third countries in terms of workplace health and safety and environmental standards, in support of the globally applicable Convention. Address ship recycling capacity The inclusion of these two facilities is an important step towards resolving the structural capacity shortage on the European List. With industry estimates pointing to a significant increase in the number of vessels reaching the end of their operational life over the coming decade, sufficient compliant recycling capacity is essential. The EU Industrial Maritime Strategy also recognises the need to pursue an international level playing field by aligning EU and global standards. A European list that reflects the reality of global recycling capacity is a precondition for the legislation to function as intended: as an incentive for safe and environmentally sound ship recycling worldwide. Compliant South Asian yards are allies, not competitors Recent data on recycling activity* shows that EU-listed yards and yards in India serve different parts of the market. EU yards recycle mainly offshore units, fishing vessels and inland ships, whereas South Asian yards recycle the large ocean-going merchant fleet. Ships recycled in the EU are also considerably smaller: EU yards handled 8% of recycled ships worldwide but only 2% of the LDT*. On average, ships recycled in the EU were only 30% of the size of the average ship recycled worldwide. The two groups of yards therefore complement each other rather than compete. EU capacity alone cannot absorb the vessels that need to be recycled in a safe and environmentally sound manner. We therefore call on Members of the European Parliament to base their decision on facts and evidence and in line with the stringent requirements of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation to support the proposal of the Commission and reject the motion for a resolution. We remain at your disposal should you have any questions. Source: European Shipowners | ECSA 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: War-related pollution: who pays?
articles.summary: Several international conventions establish strict shipowner liability backed by compulsory insurance. These include the 1992 International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage (CLC), the 2001 International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage (the Bunkers Convention) and...
articles.body: War-related pollution: who pays? in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 25/11/2026 Several international conventions establish strict shipowner liability backed by compulsory insurance. These include the 1992 International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage (CLC), the 2001 International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage (the Bunkers Convention) and the Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks. However, these conventions also contain exceptions to shipowner liability for certain war-related events. Under the 2001 Bunkers Convention, for example, the shipowner is not liable if it proves that the pollution damage resulted from an act of war, hostilities, civil war or insurrection. The same principle applies under CLC and under the Nairobi Convention. The 2010 HNS Convention, which will enter into force on 29 November 2027, follows the same logic: strict shipowner liability backed by compulsory insurance, with exclusions for acts of war, hostilities, civil war and insurrection. What does a Blue Card cover? A Blue Card is provided as evidence of the insurance or other financial security required to enable the relevant State certificate to be issued. It relates to the liabilities and financial-security requirements arising under the applicable convention. It is not an unlimited guarantee that the P&I Club will meet pollution or other costs regardless of their cause. This becomes particularly relevant where an authority asks a shipowner or its P&I Club for written confirmation that pollution response costs will be covered “regardless of the cause of the incident”, including a hostile act. Such wording may go beyond the convention liability and standard P&I cover. In effect it could amount to a request for confirmation of something that is beyond the scope of the insurance cover in that situation. The distinction between standard P&I cover and war P&I cover is well established in the marine insurance industry. Current industry guidance, for example, describes liabilities arising from incidents caused by war, hostile acts, missiles, drones, mines and similar weapons as excluded from standard P&I cover and potentially falling instead within hull war risks arrangements, which will often include war P&I cover. Will war risk insurers pay instead? Not necessarily. War risk insurance may cover P&I liabilities arising from a war peril where those liabilities would otherwise have fallen within standard P&I cover but for the war exclusion. As a general principle, however, liability cover responds only where the insured has a legal liability to pay. That is a critical feature of P&I. If the applicable convention does not impose a legal liability upon the shipowner for pollution damage resulting from an act of war, then it would follow that there may in fact be no legal liability under the convention for the relevant P&I policy to respond to. Should this be the case, there may be no liability for a war risk insurer to indemnify under the policy. There may, of course, be other exposures which can fall within the policy. A shipowner might incur response costs voluntarily, contractually, under local law or pursuant to an order from an authority. Whether those costs fall within war risks cover will depend upon the particular policy wording, the applicable law, the circumstances of the incident and the facts more generally. A shipowner facing such payments should therefore confirm with its war risk insurers whether the payment is covered. It should not be assumed that war risk cover will simply replace the standard P&I cover that would otherwise have applied. What should shipowners do? For shipowners, managers and insurance teams, there are four practical steps: • Check local requirements. A local requirement to maintain an oil spill response plan or response arrangements may not automatically engage the relevant policy to cover the corresponding costs. • Understand the nature of Blue Cards. A Blue Card relates to the liabilities and financial-security requirements arising under the applicable convention. It is not an unlimited guarantee that the P&I Club will meet pollution or other costs regardless of their cause. • Check the war risks cover. Do not assume standard P&I insurance or a convention Blue Card covers liabilities or costs caused by war risks. • Ask before giving broad confirmations. If an authority asks for proof of cover or that the scope of cover extends to hostile acts or other war risks, discuss the wording with your usual Gard contact and the relevant war risk insurer before providing any corresponding assurances. Gard can assist to confirm that a Member is entered with the Club, the scope of cover available under the applicable Rules, and how this relates to conventions with compulsory insurance requirements. However, Gard cannot provide written confirmations amounting to an expansion of that cover or which may convert a convention Blue Card into something more like an all-risks pollution guarantee. Source: Gard, https://www.gard.no/en/insights/war-related-pollution-who-pays/ 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Tresco Group acquires Green Maritime and sets course for seagoing shipping in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 Tresco, the Antwerp-based leader in inland navigation software backed by Strada Partners, has acquired Green Maritime, the Dutch specialist in operational data on board seagoing vessels. Green Maritime’s technology runs on 220 vessels today, mainly in short sea shipping. The deal takes Tresco beyond inland waterways into the much larger seagoing market, where EU climate rules are driving demand for measured fuel and emissions data. It is the next step in Tresco’s ambition to build a broad maritime technology group, through organic growth and targeted acquisitions. Measured data, straight from on board Green Maritime collects on-board data on fuel consumption, engine performance and navigation. Shipowners use it to report emissions, cut fuel costs, spot technical problems early and run their fleets more efficiently. The system is affordable and quick to install. Instead of calculating with bunker delivery notes and estimates, it measures what a ship actually burns. Proven in daily operation on 220 vessels, it is ready to scale. Former sea captain Bart Schut founded Green Maritime in 2020, after seven years at sea and five years running operations at a shipping company. He built the platform around the problems he ran into on board and in the office. Photo (© Tresco Group): Bart Schut, founder and CEO of Green Maritime; Johan Van Ommen, COO of Green Maritime; Evert Bulcke, CEO of Tresco Group; and Cedric Peeters, Head of Finance at Tresco Group. More images are available on request. Regulation drives demand Since 2024, seagoing vessels of 5,000 GT and above fall under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). The scheme is being phased in: for emissions from 2026 onwards, shipowners must surrender allowances for 100% of their verified emissions. FuelEU Maritime has applied since 1 January 2025 and lowers the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy used on board step by step. By the end of 2026, the European Commission will assess whether to extend the rules to smaller ships, which could bring short sea vessels and coasters below 5,000 GT into scope. Both systems rest on accurate measurement. A shipowner who doesn’t know what a ship burns can’t report its emissions correctly, let alone reduce them. The same data keeps fuel costs in check and shows how a fleet performs, so the investment pays off well beyond compliance. “Regulation is driving innovation in the maritime sector,” said Evert Bulcke, CEO of Tresco Group. “The rules are mostly European, but their impact reaches far beyond Europe. Emissions reporting is only as good as the operational data underneath it. That sounds simpler than it is: a ship is not a car. It’s a complex system.” Building a broad maritime technology group Tresco equips some 9,000 vessels in European inland shipping with navigation and automation software. Green Maritime opens up a much larger market: thousands of short sea vessels will need emissions monitoring and better operational data in the coming years. Over time, Tresco will bring its inland and seagoing data together on one platform, giving customers a single view of their fleet on inland waterways and at sea. “Green Maritime gives us a strong position in seagoing shipping, with a product that has proven itself on 220 vessels,” said Bulcke. “The value in maritime technology lies in reliable data on board, a strong market share and deep knowledge of the sector. You don’t copy that with AI. We see room to double the number of connected vessels, and that’s before we look at Southeast Asia.” Matthias Vandepitte, Managing Partner at Strada Partners and Board Member at Tresco Group: “When we invested in Tresco in 2024, the plan was clear: build on its leadership in inland navigation to create a broad maritime technology group. Green Maritime fits that plan perfectly, with proven technology, a founder who knows the sector from the bridge, and a market that regulation is opening up fast. We’re excited to back Evert and Bart in this next chapter.” What changes for customers Green Maritime will remain a separate business unit, led from Apeldoorn by founder and CEO Bart Schut. Seagoing shipping has its own market, language and way of working, so integration will happen step by step. The full team is joining. Existing customers keep their contacts and their service, and gain access to Tresco’s European installation and dealer network and to the group’s R&D capacity. “Our customers are asking for scale: more vessels, faster installations and deeper integration with the systems on board,” said Bart Schut, founder and CEO of Green Maritime. “Tresco brings thirty years of experience with on-board software and an installation network across Europe. Together we can grow faster in short sea and take our product further.” Source: Tresco Group 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

The deal takes Tresco beyond inland waterways into the much larger seagoing market, where EU climate rules are driving demand for measured fuel and emissions data.
It is the next step in Tresco’s ambition to build a broad maritime technology group, through organic growth and targeted acquisitions.

articles.body: ENGINE: East of Suez Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 25/11/2026 Singapore and Malaysia Bunker fuel availability remains tight in Singapore, with terminal loading slots and barge capacity largely booked through November for most suppliers. Some suppliers have also begun receiving bookings for December deliveries, a source said. VLSFO lead times have shortened to 12-14 days, from 15-17 days last week. HSFO lead times are around 10 days, compared with 9-12 days previously. LSMGO availability has improved more significantly, with lead times falling to 5-8 days, from 12-14 days. In Malaysia, supply remains constrained across all major fuel grades at Port Klang. Prompt VLSFO availability is particularly limited, while LSMGO supplies are tight for prompt deliveries. HSFO availability also remains restricted. East Asia Bunker fuel availability in Zhoushan has improved slightly as subdued demand and a reduced backlog ease pressure on supplies, a source said. Lead times have fallen to around seven days, from nine days last week. Supply conditions remain mixed across other Chinese ports. Dalian and Qingdao have sufficient VLSFO and LSMGO supplies, although HSFO availability remains tight in Qingdao. All three major fuel grades are in tight supply in Tianjin, while VLSFO and HSFO availability remains limited in Shanghai. LSMGO supplies in Shanghai, however, are relatively stable. Supply constraints also persist in southern China. Suppliers in Fuzhou, Yangpu and Guangzhou are reporting shortages of both VLSFO and LSMGO. Xiamen, by contrast, has good availability of both grades. Bunker supply in Hong Kong remains stable, with suppliers recommending lead times of around seven days for the major fuel grades. In Taiwan, VLSFO and LSMGO lead times remain largely unchanged at around two days across Keelung, Taichung, Kaohsiung and Hualien. Prompt availability has tightened slightly across several South Korean ports. At southern ports, including Busan, Ulsan, Masan, Onsan, Yeosu and Kwangyang, lead times for all major fuel grades have increased to 5-8 days from 3-7 days last week. A similar increase in lead times has been reported at western ports, including Incheon, Daesan, Dangjin, Pyeongtaek and Taean, where VLSFO, LSMGO and HSFO lead times are also around 5-8 days. Adverse weather could further disrupt bunker operations at several South Korean ports in the coming days. Operations in Busan and Ulsan may be affected during 24-26 and 28-29 November. Yeosu could face disruptions during 24-25 and 28-29 November, while operations in Daesan may be interrupted between 24-30 November. VLSFO availability remains severely constrained at several Japanese ports, including Tokyo, Chiba, Kawasaki, Nagoya, Yokkaichi, Osaka, Kobe, Mizushima, Tokuyama and Oita. Supplies at these locations are available on an enquiry basis. HSFO and LSMGO availability, however, remains normal. Both VLSFO and HSFO supplies are tight in Kashima. Indonesia continues to buck the tighter supply trend across much of East Asia, with bunker fuel availability generally healthy. Suppliers in Jakarta, Surabaya, Balikpapan and Cigading typically recommend VLSFO lead times of just 2-3 days. Oceania Bunker fuel availability remains stable in Western Australia, with VLSFO readily available in Kwinana and Fremantle. Suppliers at both ports recommend lead times of around seven days. Each port has only one supplier, and all bunker deliveries are carried out by barge. Supply conditions are more varied along Australia’s east coast. Port Kembla has normal VLSFO availability, with deliveries possible by truck or pipeline. Sydney has sufficient stocks of VLSFO and LSMGO, although HSFO availability is tighter, requiring suppliers to be given around seven days’ notice. Brisbane and Gladstone have ample VLSFO and LSMGO supplies, with lead times of approximately one week. VLSFO availability has also improved in Melbourne and Geelong. However, HSFO supply has tightened further in Melbourne and Brisbane. The upcoming cyclone season could pose a risk to bunker operations across Australia, a source said. Running from November through April, the season could disrupt fuel availability and deliveries at ports nationwide. New Zealand’s bunker market remains broadly stable. VLSFO is readily available in Tauranga and Auckland, where suppliers recommend lead times of around four days. At Marsden Point, vessels can receive VLSFO and LSMGO directly through pipelines. Adverse weather remains the main operational concern in New Zealand, particularly in Wellington and ports across the South Island, where disruptions to marine operations could delay bunker deliveries. In Papua New Guinea, LSMGO availability remains tight in Rabaul, Madang and Lae. South Asia Suppliers recommend lead times of around 2-3 days for VLSFO, HSFO and LSMGO at several major Indian ports, including Kandla, Cochin, Paradip, Visakhapatnam, Kakinada, Haldia, Chennai, Tuticorin and New Mangalore, according to an India-based source. In Mumbai, LSMGO availability remains tight, while VLSFO and HSFO supplies are readily available. In Sri Lanka, lead times for all major fuel grades at Colombo have shortened to around seven days from 7-11 days last week. Middle East Bunker demand in the Arab Gulf remains subdued amid ongoing regional tensions and increased attacks around the Strait of Hormuz, a Middle East-based trader said. In Fujairah, VLSFO and LSMGO are readily available, while HSFO supply remains tight, a regional source said. Bunker demand in Saudi Arabia has declined significantly. In Jeddah, LSMGO availability remains generally stable, while VLSFO supplies continue to be constrained. Demand remains healthy at Omani ports. LSMGO deliveries at Salalah, Sohar, Duqm and Muscat can generally be arranged within 2-3 days. In Qatar, supplies of both VLSFO and LSMGO remain restricted at Ras Laffan. Meanwhile, Port Suez in Egypt is experiencing low inventories across all major bunker fuel grades. Djibouti also continues to face limited availability of all three major bunker fuel grades. Source: By Tuhin Roy, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news 2026-11-25 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: COSCO SHIPPING Specialized Carriers has launched a new direct Ro-Ro service connecting Xiaomo Port in Shenzhen with Astakos Port in Greece. The service began with the departure of the Ro-Ro vessel Yuan He Kou, carrying 4,898 Chinese-made new energy vehicles from Xiaomo to the Greek port. The vessel is expected to complete the voyage in approximately 20 days. The new connection reduces transit time by nearly one-third compared with conventional services. The inaugural shipment includes several electric vehicle models, including the BYD Seagull, Sealion and Dolphin. Following discharge at Astakos, the vehicles will be distributed through feeder connections to Zeebrugge in Belgium, Koper in Slovenia and Valencia in Spain. This network will provide onward access to automotive markets across the Mediterranean and wider Europe. The route is Xiaomo Port’s first direct foreign-trade Ro-Ro connection with Greece and expands the port’s growing vehicle shipping network. Xiaomo Port has developed into an important export gateway for new energy vehicles manufactured in Shenzhen and the surrounding region. The port plans to expand its domestic and international services while strengthening its vehicle-handling and logistics capabilities.

articles.title: BUILT TO LAST: BRISTOL HARBOR GROUP, INC. & THE SHEARER GROUP, INC. BECOME EMPLOYEE OWNED
articles.summary: Two established naval architecture and marine engineering firms become 100% employee owned, carrying forward the vision and values of their founders. Bristol Harbor Group, Inc. (BHGI) and The Shearer Group,...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Two established naval architecture and marine engineering firms become 100% employee owned, carrying forward the vision and values of their founders. Bristol Harbor Group, Inc. (BHGI) and The Shearer Group, Inc. (TSGI) are proud to announce that both companies are now 100% employee owned through an Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP), marking an important milestone for the two naval architecture and marine engineering firms. For Gregory W. Beers, P.E., and Cory C. Wood, who founded BHGI in 1995 and later established TSGI in 2010, the transition represents the continuation of a vision that began more than three decades ago: to build the most well-respected naval architecture and marine engineering firms in the industry. Gregory and Cory have spent decades building BHGI and TSGI with a vision that extends well beyond their own leadership. Through careful planning, the development of strong management teams, and a continued investment in their employees, they have positioned both firms to become multigenerational leaders in the naval architecture and marine engineering industry. The transition to employee ownership is a significant step in securing that future, ensuring that the companies they founded continue to grow and succeed for generations to come. While ownership has changed, both firms will continue operating much as they have for years. Gregory and Cory will remain at the forefront of both companies, providing leadership and direction alongside their established management teams. Clients can continue to expect the same level of service and technical expertise from the employees they’ve come to know and trust over the years. BHGI’s History BHGI traces its origins back to 1993, when Gregory and Cory, along with Andy Tyska of Bristol Marine and another fellow student at the University of Michigan Naval Architecture and Marine Engineering Department set out to design a passenger vessel while still in school. Their first design, the STAR OF SAUGATUCK II , marked an early milestone for the firm and is still operating on the Kalamazoo River in Southwest Michigan. Building on that early initiative, the group formally incorporated BHGI in 1995, and the firm has continued to grow in Bristol, Rhode Island, ever since. Over the years, BHGI has developed into a close-knit team of 19, maintaining a hands-on, collaborative working environment. Today, the engineering team is led by Daniel P. Eling, P.E. For more than three decades, BHGI has been guided by a set of core values established early on by Greg and Cory. Those values continue to shape the firm’s work today and center on technical excellence, attention to detail, a strong focus on clients, engineering ethics, professionalism, and responsibility. TSGI’s History In 2010, Gregory and Cory formed The Shearer Group, Inc. (TSGI), a sister company to BHGI located in Houston, Texas. The company was established when Gregory and Cory purchased the assets of Shearer & Assoc., Inc. from Edward L. Shearer, P.E., its founder and president. The three had heard of one another through industry connections and eventually met at a SNAME convention. That encounter led to further discussions, and ultimately the formation of TSGI. The “Shearer” name has long been associated with the inland marine industry, reflecting both Ed’s contributions to naval architecture and his family’s multigenerational barge line. When TSGI was established, it brought together Ed’s years of experience at Shearer & Associates, Inc. and the naval architecture and marine engineering expertise Gregory and Cory had developed at BHGI. Ed remains involved as a Principal Naval Architect. Today, TSGI provides marine engineering services to clients in the inland and offshore marine industries. The firm offers many of the same services as BHGI, along with additional services suited to its Houston location, including marine surveying and OSHA-compliant maritime gear certification support. As TSGI continued to grow, Joshua S. Sebastian, P.E., joined the firm in 2013, bringing five years of engineering experience at BHGI, along with his nine-year background as an officer in the U.S. Coast Guard. He relocated to Texas to serve as Engineering Manager, as part of Gregory and Cory’s plan to build TSGI with the same technical and cultural approach used at BHGI. In 2022, Joshua stepped into the role of Vice President – Operations, with Senior Naval Architect Harrison C. Brann, P.E., stepping into the role of Engineering Manager. Over 15 years, TSGI has grown into another close-knit team of 19. Under Joshua and Harrison’s leadership, TSGI has continued to grow while maintaining the same approach and core principles established at BHGI. Today, the firm remains dedicated to serving vessels that operate on the inland waterways and continuing the tradition established by its namesake. articles.title: Port of Brisbane rolls out green button functionality
articles.summary: The Port of Brisbane has made its Green Button functionality available for deep draft vessel movements, meaning vessels with a draft exceeding 12 metres, within its 90-kilometre shipping channel. The tool is designed to maximise vessel efficiency and minimise emissions by identifying optimal transit speed profiles...
articles.body: The Port of Brisbane has made its Green Button functionality available for deep draft vessel movements, meaning vessels with a draft exceeding 12 metres, within its 90-kilometre shipping channel. The tool is designed to maximise vessel efficiency and minimise emissions by identifying optimal transit speed profiles that reduce fuel consumption within designated arrival and departure windows. It draws on forecast wind, currents, tides and water depth to calculate efficient transit plans and to estimate potential emissions reductions against standard operating profiles. Green Button is the latest addition to the Nonlinear Channel Optimisation Simulator (NCOS) Online, developed with DHI Seaport, following the release of enhanced planning and weather modules earlier this year. NCOS Online has been in use at the port since 2017 and provides a seven-day detailed forecast of a vessel’s under keel clearance and environmental conditions, allowing dynamic scheduling. It enables stakeholders including the Regional Harbour Master to determine safely and accurately the clearance needed for larger vessels, and it is also used to inform safe operating and environmental parameters for some landside operations. Port of Brisbane CEO Neil Stephens described the Green Button as world-class, leading-edge technology developed in Brisbane that offers a chance to cut shipping-related emissions while keeping vessel scheduling safe, reliable and effective. Following highly successful trials in 2024, it is now enabled to support stakeholders planning and managing deep draft movements. Stephens said the continued development of NCOS Online reflects the aspiration for Brisbane to become a more efficient, connected and sustainable port, and thanked DHI Seaport, Maritime Safety Queensland’s Regional Harbour Master, Poseidon Sea Pilots and shipping line customers Maersk and CMA CGM for their collaboration during the trial and implementation phases.

articles.body: Ukraine Strikes Russian Ship in Gulf of Finland Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 24, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Peter Hermes Furian Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy confirmed his country was responsible for Saturday's drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland, while Norway, a strong supporter of Kyiv, urged it to exercise caution in such operations. Finnish, Estonian and Russian vessels took part in a joint rescue operation to put out the fire. On Sunday, a Russian vessel towed the ship back into Russian waters, where it is now anchored in St Petersburg. Zelenskiy said the operation had struck a legitimate military target. "We did everything right," Zelenskiy told Bloomberg on Monday. "Every vessel with a Russian flag, everything that carries weapons or any sanctioned cargo that can carry God knows what, it is a legitimate target for us in Russian territorial or neutral waters." The Sparta II is a Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Oboronlogistika, a Russian shipping company providing logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry, according to the company's website. Zelenskiy said the attack occurred in Russian territorial waters. "We had all the rights for that and then some drift happened and surely there are questions," he said. He acknowledged that some European allies were "worried when something is happening in the Baltic Sea" and said he had instructed his ministers and the military to "communicate more with partners so that they have enough details and there are no surprises". 'NEED FOR STABILITY IN OUR NEAR AREAS' Norwegian Defence Minister Tore Sandvik said on Tuesday there was an ongoing dialogue with Ukraine regarding "a need for stability in our near areas". "All attacks would stop immediately if Russia stopped this war. That said, we are focused on the fact that Ukraine must do this (these actions) within the rules of international law. So we take this matter up with them," Sandvik told reporters. "We are also focused on the fact that they must respect our need for stability in our near areas and we have a good dialogue with the Ukrainians on that now," he added. Sandvik was speaking after signing an agreement with his Ukrainian counterpart, Yevhenii Khmara, to expand bilateral cooperation on an anti-drone system in order to increase its use in more parts of Ukraine. Russian forces have been subjecting Kyiv and other cities to virtually continuous air attacks since September. Sandvik did not say whether he had discussed the Gulf of Finland attack with Khmara at their meeting. NATO member Norway has set up a long-term funding plan for Ukraine, with the backing of all parties in parliament, amounting to some $27 billion between 2023 and 2030, making it one of Kyiv's most generous backers per capita. (Reuters)

articles.title: Maersk and ONE Eye Landmark Global North-South Shipping Alliance
articles.summary: The formation of container shipping’s first global liner alliance covering the north-south trades appears to be taking shape, The Loadstar has learned.

Join the leading maritime news network Containers are seen on the Maersk's Triple-E giant container ship Majestic Maersk, one of the world's largest container ships, next to cranes at the APM Terminals in the port of Algeciras, Spain January 20, 2023. REUTERS/Jon Nazca/File Photo By Nils Roche (The Loadstar) – The formation of container shipping’s first global liner alliance covering the north-south trades appears to be taking shape, The Loadstar has learned. Container lines have traditionally treated the north-south trades as a set of separate marriages, on the assumption that the right partner depends on the trade. However, according to sources in Asia, Maersk and Ocean Network Express (ONE) are working to develop a vessel-sharing agreement (VSA) covering the trades globally, rather than lane by lane. The Loadstar has approached both carriers for comment but has yet to receive a formal response, and the form the VDSA would take is unclear. Nonetheless, if confirmed it would be the first VSA of its kind – and its logic rests on ONE’s fleet, according to our provisional analysis below. Their respective groupings, the Gemini Cooperation for Maersk and Premier Alliance for ONE, stop at east-west trades, while north-south has remained a patchwork of classic VSAs, where each carrier’s slots follow the ships it provides, and an agreement rarely covers more than two or three services. Why not Hapag-Lloyd? The obvious choice of partner for Maersk would be Hapag-Lloyd, its Gemini compatriot – but two things rule it out. The first is that CSAV owns 30% of it and sits in the shareholder pact that controls more than 70% of the carrier, so combining West Coast South America networks would join two incumbents serving the same Chilean and Peruvian exporters. In that context, it is worth noting that Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd do not cooperate on any of their respective Asia-WC South America services – according to Xeneta’s eeSea liner database, Maersk operates two standalone strings, the AC1 and AC3, while Hapag-Lloyd’s three offerings are run in cooperation with MSC, HMM, and ONE. Secondly, Hapag-Lloyd has relatively few ships coming – its orderbook is 19% of its fleet, the lowest of the eight largest carriers, on trades where Far East–Latin America capacity grew 14% in a year. ONE poses fewer of those problems. On Far East–WC South America, for example, Linerlytica puts Maersk at 16.1% of weekly capacity and ONE at 9%; together a quarter of the trade, ahead of CMA CGM and MSC, from two carriers whose customers overlap less. The ships are the point ONE has the fleet those trades are moving towards. Alphaliner puts 36% of its operated capacity in ships of 10,000–15,100 teu, against 14% at Maersk. Of the 55 ships ONE has on order, 29 – representing 60% of the total 647,000 teu expected – fall in the same bracket. Linerlytica puts the average ship on Far East–Latin America already at 10,032 teu. However, only 10 of ONE’s 62 ships in that class currently work Latin American routes. Under the classic formula, ships buy slots, so tonnage converts directly into share. A global partner gives ONE’s newbuilds work without ONE building Latin American and African franchises alone. Maersk, whose next order according to Linerlytica is for 24,000 teu ships, would thus get mid-size capacity without ordering it. What it will probably look like “Global” may describe the scope more than the mechanics. North-south shippers pay for direct calls, Brazil reserves feeder legs for Brazilian-flag operators, and Mexico’s ports do little relay business. That points to core loops on one carrier’s ships where its fleet fits, and shared loops where the ship mix demands it, rather than a Gemini-style hub network. The obstacles are real. Hapag-Lloyd sits alongside ONE in several of these consortia, so the deal means reordering them with Maersk’s own Gemini partner, and a quarter of Asia–WC South America capacity will interest regulators in Chile and Peru. And similar disentanglements will be necessary on other north-south trades: for example, Maersk continues to cooperate with CMA CGM on Asia-West Africa services. And although there were rumours that that cooperation might be coming to an end, they have subsided for now. The quay question… …will be where ONE’s 13,724 teu newbuilds are deployed in 2027. The industry has assumed north-south partners must be chosen trade by trade. A Maersk–ONE framework tests a different premise: that the scarce input is the right ship, and a carrier holding them can be a partner almost everywhere. Photo courtesy HD Hyundai The state-owned Shipping Corporation of India (SCI) is seeking to acquire up to 22 new vessels in a multibillion-dollar fleet expansion that could provide a major boost to India’s domestic shipbuilding industry. The procurement program spans some of the largest and most sophisticated vessels in commercial shipping, including ultra-large containerships, very large gas carriers (VLGCs) and Suezmax crude oil tankers. According to SCI’s official tender notices , the program includes eight VLGCs, six 18,000-TEU containerships, two Suezmax tankers and up to six 8,000-TEU containerships, including four optional vessels. The combined newbuilding program could be worth as much as $3.2 billion, according to India’s Economic Times. shipindia.com+2 Significantly, the tenders are structured to encourage international shipbuilders to establish manufacturing facilities in India or enter into technical partnerships with domestic shipyards. Under the VLGC tender, two vessels would be constructed at an established overseas shipyard, with the remaining six built in India. A similar arrangement calls for four of the six 18,000-TEU containerships to be constructed domestically. Indian shipyards would also receive the right of first refusal to match competing foreign bids for the smaller containerships and Suezmax tankers. Four of the six ultra-large containerships are earmarked for the proposed Bharat Container Shipping Line, part of India’s broader effort to expand its presence in global container shipping and reduce reliance on foreign carriers. SCI is separately seeking to acquire up to four secondhand containerships ranging from 1,500 to 2,500 TEU in capacity. The procurement drive comes as India pursues an ambitious goal of becoming one of the world’s five largest shipbuilding nations by 2047. The government has been courting major South Korean shipbuilders, including HD Hyundai, Samsung Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean, to invest in domestic shipbuilding capacity. Bids for the containerships and Suezmax tankers are due in December, followed by the VLGC tender in January 2027. While the vessels have yet to be ordered, the scale and structure of the procurement program underscore India’s intention to use state-backed shipping demand to develop a globally competitive shipbuilding industry. articles.title: Ex-Petrofac Executives on Trial After Alleged Bribes
articles.summary: Two former executives at British oilfield services provider Petrofac were involved in the payment of bribes to secure multibillion-dollar contracts in the United Arab Emirates, prosecutors said at the start of their trial on Tuesday.Marwan Chedid…
articles.body: Ex-Petrofac Executives on Trial After Alleged Bribes Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 24, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Lukasz Z Two former executives at British oilfield services provider Petrofac were involved in the payment of bribes to secure multibillion-dollar contracts in the United Arab Emirates, prosecutors said at the start of their trial on Tuesday. Marwan Chedid, Petrofac's former chief operating officer, and George Salibi, chief operating officer of Petrofac's engineering and construction division, are both charged with two counts of bribery which allegedly took place between 2012 and 2018 relating to the Upper Zakum offshore oilfield. Prosecutors allege the pair were involved in corrupt schemes to secure contracts worth around $3.4 billion with the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), with around $23 million in bribes paid and disguised using false invoices and third-party companies. Chedid and Salibi both pleaded not guilty ahead of their trial at London's Southwark Crown Court. Prosecutor Jonathan Kinnear said the bribes were paid through an agent called Basim Al-Shaikh, a British national who died in 2021. He added the defendants seemed to accept that payments were made but disputed that they were bribes or that they knew bribes were being paid. The first bribery charge relates to a contract to expand the capacity of the Upper Zakum oilfield to 750,000 barrels per day, with the second count relating to a variation order to increase capacity to 1 million bpd. Kinnear said bribes were paid via Al-Shaikh to other intermediaries and then on to people linked to ADNOC who were "able to assist Petrofac with their bid". Chedid and Salibi were aware of the sums paid to Al-Shaikh and there was "no legitimate or any other commercial reason for disguising the payment of money", Kinnear told the jury. "This sustained exercise of concealment is at the very heart of the case," Kinnear added. "If the defendants ... knew that payments were being made to Basim (Al-Shaikh) under the cover of false purchase orders or invoices and by way of the other underhand, indirect methods ... that is, we say, powerful evidence that they were fully aware of and participating in the offering, giving and paying of bribes." Kinnear also said that a more junior ex-Petrofac employee, David Lufkin, had previously pleaded guilty to bribery offences in relation to the Upper Zakum contracts and would give evidence for the prosecution. The trial continues and is due to conclude in March. (Reuters)

French authorities have successfully refloated the Malta-flagged bulk carrier MIRO G , four days after the vessel ran aground on France’s Atlantic coast during severe weather. The Atlantic Maritime Prefecture confirmed Tuesday afternoon that the complex salvage operation had succeeded in freeing the vessel from a beach near Lit-et-Mixe in the Landes department of southwestern France. The operation involved extensive maritime, land and aerial resources, bringing together French military personnel, government agencies and private-sector salvage specialists, including Les Abeilles International. Following the successful refloating, the French Navy deployed a Falcon 50 maritime surveillance aircraft to assess the environmental situation. No marine pollution was detected at the grounding site or along the vessel’s subsequent transit route. The MIRO G will now be taken under the care of tugs mobilized by the Port of Bordeaux for onward transit to Le Verdon, where divers will conduct an underwater inspection of the vessel’s hull to assess any damage.
