November 24, 2026 © Adobe Stock/le Oil prices edged higher on Tuesday in a choppy session as new attacks were reported on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, but gains were capped by an outlook for surplus global supplies. Brent crude futures bounced off a session trough that was their lowest since August 27 and were up 45 cents, or 0.5%, to $89.82 a barrel at 11:25 a.m. EDT (1625 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up 42 cents, or 0.52%, at $80.59 a barrel. Their session low was the weakest since August 10. Brent's session low was $88.10 a barrel, while WTI slipped as low as $79.07, pressured by a stock market slide. On Monday, three vessels were struck by unidentified projectiles as they sailed east through the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Tuesday. All three vessels continued their journeys and all crew members were accounted for, UKMTO said. "Expectations for excess supply continue to restrain the recovery, leaving crude sensitive to whether further attacks actually interrupt deliveries," Gelber & Associates analysts said in a note. The US is investigating whether Iran was involved in cyberattacks on as many as 50 energy tankers, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing US officials and others familiar with the matter. SUPPLY SIGNALS Libya's Sharara oil pipeline has reopened after an "unlawful group" closed a valve on the pipeline, and oil has begun to flow into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya, the chairperson of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Monday. China and India are on track for record Russian oil imports this year, plugging a supply gap caused by the Iran war, according to tanker data and industry insiders. Temporary US waivers on Russian oil sanctions widened the pool of vessels and suppliers available to India and China, allowing them to increase purchases at a time when supplies from the Middle East are disrupted. But sustained Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure tempered available supplies. Russia will "inevitably" respond to the continuing Ukrainian attacks on its refineries, President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday, adding he wanted the government to discuss additional security measures for energy facilities. Putin noted that US President Donald Trump had explicitly asked Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries. The overall global oil supply outlook still was seen as a surplus. Deutsche Bank said that global observed liquids inventories rose in October, implying an oversupply of 1.7 million barrels per day. Evidence is accumulating that the global market is rebalancing and turning into surplus, although setbacks could delay progress, the bank said in a research report. US crude oil and product inventories likely rose last week, a preliminary Reuters poll showed. "Oil prices are facing modest downward pressure from two sides: markets are pricing out some near-term geopolitical risk in the Middle East, while releases from strategic reserves are keeping supply relatively comfortable despite lower regional exports and stronger Chinese demand," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo. Elsewhere, Iraq's prime minister has ordered the federal oil ministry to manage oilfields in areas under Kurdish security control, the state news agency said on Tuesday, potentially deepening tensions between Baghdad and the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region. REUTERS/Stringer Four more commercial vessels have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz, bringing the number of reported tanker strikes in the strategic waterway to 10 in a single week, as Iran expands its crackdown to maritime service providers assisting vessels it deems non-compliant. The latest warnings from United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) detail attacks against three tankers and a bulk carrier on November 22, underscoring the persistent threat to commercial shipping nearly nine months into the Iran war. The three tankers were struck by unidentified projectiles while transiting eastbound through the Strait of Hormuz. All three vessels continued their voyages, with all crew members accounted for. The extent of damage and any environmental impact remain unknown. UKMTO initially reported the tanker strikes under a single warning before reclassifying them as three separate attacks. In a separate incident, a bulk carrier at anchor off Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates, was struck by an unidentified projectile, triggering an onboard fire. No casualties were reported. The identities of the four vessels have not been disclosed. The latest attacks follow a sustained series of strikes against outbound tankers near Oman’s Musandam Peninsula. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), in its November 22 advisory, reported that seven tankers had been struck in the Strait of Hormuz since November 16. The three subsequently reported tanker attacks bring that tally to 10. Among the earlier incidents were attacks against the tankers Torkel and Arina on November 21. JMIC continues to assess the maritime threat level in the Strait of Hormuz as severe, warning that further deliberate attacks are highly likely. Iranian claims that tankers have been struck by mines have not been independently confirmed. Iran Widens Shipping Blacklist to Tugs Meanwhile, Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) announced that it had added 26 tugboats to its list of non-compliant vessels, accusing them of providing services to ships operating in violation of its restrictions in the southern Strait of Hormuz. The authority said the tugboats had been identified through intelligence monitoring and reports from citizens in Iran’s southern neighboring countries, reiterating that vessels and companies assisting ships deemed non-compliant would themselves face blacklisting. According to maritime security analyst Martin Kelly of Orbital Risk Intelligence, Iran’s non-compliance list already contained 240 vessels as of November 19, potentially bringing the total to 266 with the latest additions. The move signals a widening of Tehran’s efforts to exert control over commercial shipping, and raises particular concerns for towing and salvage operators at a time when repeated attacks have left a growing number of vessels damaged or disabled. In its November 20 assessment, Orbital warned that further Iranian attacks on merchant vessels were highly likely over the following week, while prospects for a U.S.-Iran agreement that would end attacks on shipping remained slim. The firm also said it had seen no evidence to substantiate repeated Iranian claims that tankers had struck naval mines in the Strait. IMO Confirms 141 Incidents, 25 Seafarer Deaths The latest attacks come as the International Maritime Organization’s tally of confirmed maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and wider Middle East reached 141 as of November 23, with 25 confirmed seafarer fatalities. Among the latest vessels identified by the IMO are Captain Leon , Bahra and On Phoenix , all of which suffered damage in incidents near Oman in recent days. The four vessels involved in Sunday’s attacks have yet to appear individually on the IMO’s published list, and it remains unclear whether the latest attacks are already reflected in the organization’s cumulative tally. Hormuz Traffic Remains Depressed Despite an increase in U.S.-facilitated transits in recent days, commercial shipping activity through the Strait of Hormuz remains well below pre-war levels. According to JMIC, 114 vessels completed U.S.-facilitated transits between November 19 and 21, averaging 38 per day, up from 27 per day during the preceding four days. That compares with a historical average of approximately 138 daily vessel transits in 2025. Separately, commercial vessel tracking recorded no AIS-visible transits by qualifying cargo-carrying vessels outside the U.S.-facilitated traffic figures during the three-day period, although the data excludes certain Iranian port traffic. Approximately 218 commercial vessels remained stationary at major anchorages east of the Strait as of November 22, with JMIC expecting the backlog to persist. The renewed attacks and Iran’s widening crackdown highlight the continuing challenges facing efforts to restore commercial navigation through the world’s most important oil shipping chokepoint, even as the United States continues to facilitate vessel passages and enforce its blockade of Iranian ports. articles.title: NX Group invests in Sun Metalon to develop recycling logistics network
articles.summary: Nippon Express Holdings (NX Group) has signed a capital and business alliance agreement with Sun Metalon, a metal recycling technology company, as part of plans to develop new logistics services for recycled industrial materials. The Japanese logistics group acquired a stake in Sun Metalon on 31 October 2026 through...
articles.body: Nippon Express Holdings (NX Group) has signed a capital and business alliance agreement with Sun Metalon, a metal recycling technology company, as part of plans to develop new logistics services for recycled industrial materials. The Japanese logistics group acquired a stake in Sun Metalon on 31 October 2026 through its NX Global Innovation Investment Fund. The investment was announced on 24 November. The partnership will combine Sun Metalon’s recycling technology with NX Group’s logistics network to develop supply chains connecting metal scrap collection, processing and the supply of recycled materials to manufacturers. The companies aim to support industrial customers seeking to recover valuable materials from manufacturing waste and return them to production. Building a recycling logistics network Founded in 2021, Sun Metalon operates in Japan and the United States and specialises in technology for recycling metal scrap generated during manufacturing. Its Venus recycling equipment uses proprietary heating technology to remove oil and moisture from metal cutting and grinding waste. The process produces recycled metal material without mixing or melting the original scrap, allowing it to be reused as a raw material in metal production. Under the agreement, NX Group and Sun Metalon plan to establish an integrated logistics network connecting manufacturing facilities, recycling operations and metal producers. The companies will explore the development of a wider network linking multiple processing facilities with steelmakers and casting manufacturers. NX Group will also examine opportunities to develop specialised equipment for collecting, storing and transporting metal materials. Additional services could include transporting, installing and leasing recycling equipment to industrial customers. Partnership targets circular supply chains The agreement comes as manufacturers seek to increase the use of recycled materials and reduce the environmental impact of industrial production. Sun Metalon’s technology is designed to recover higher-value scrap that can serve as a raw material for electric arc furnaces. NX Group expects its transport infrastructure and customer network to support the wider adoption of the technology across manufacturing supply chains. The companies will also work on services allowing manufacturers to recover metal scrap from their facilities and return the processed materials to industrial production. The partnership is expected to support resource recycling activities in Japan and the United States. NX Group has not disclosed the financial value of its investment or the size of its ownership stake in Sun Metalon. No implementation timetable or specific customer contracts for the proposed recycling logistics network have been announced.

articles.summary: When OPEC+ oil ministers gather at the end of this month to figure out how much crude to supply the world, they’ll face their most consequential decision of the year.

REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian By Grant Smith, Nayla Razzouk and Salma El Wardany (Bloomberg) — When OPEC + oil ministers gather at the end of this month to figure out how much crude to supply the world, they’ll face their most consequential decision of the year. Saudi Arabia and its partners must plot a course for 2027, positioning themselves for the potential end of the Iran war while contending with strains inside the alliance. The United Arab Emirates has already quit after years of frustration with its production limits and Iraq has pushed for room to pump more. Integral to the talks, ministers will have to digest the results of the most comprehensive external review yet of how much each member is capable of producing, a highly sensitive exercise whose findings have so far been kept closely guarded even within OPEC+. The review, completed this month by Dallas-based consultants DeGolyer and MacNaughton Corp., seeks to put an independent number on one of the most contentious questions inside the alliance: each country’s maximum sustainable oil production capacity. Those numbers matter because they will form a new starting point for countries’ future production targets. In simple terms, the greater the capacity assigned to a country, the stronger its claim to be allowed to pump more. Yet even after the exercise concluded, members weren’t given the full picture. Countries received their own results, while OPEC+ didn’t circulate a list showing the capacity assigned to every member, according to delegates. That leaves governments heading into the meeting without knowing precisely how their capabilities stack up against their peers. The meeting of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies comes at a time of extraordinary uncertainty in the market: Will the world pump more barrels of oil each day next year than it consumes, as organizations like the International Energy Agency predict? Will rivals such as the US and Guyana keep ramping up? Will demand hold up — or even snap back — in 2027 if the war is resolved? And will consumer governments seek to replenish stockpiles heavily depleted by the conflict? “OPEC+ faces an extremely difficult call for 2027,” said Jorge Leon, head of geopolitical analysis at Rystad Energy who previously worked at the OPEC secretariat. “The group has to plan around huge uncertainty over the US-Iran war, the pace of recovery through the Strait of Hormuz, and the size of the surplus that could emerge once disrupted barrels return.” The most immediate stakes are oil prices. Brent futures have tumbled almost 25% this month as the Saudis and other Persian Gulf exporters managed to shift barrels out of the region at pre-war rates despite the ongoing hostilities. Physical markets look comfortably supplied and a renewed surplus next year could erode revenues for the petro-states that compose OPEC+. While Sunday’s meeting will be consequential for the group’s overall production policy for 2027, the impact on the short-term supply of oil will probably be more modest. Despite this month’s plunge, prices are still up by about 40% compared with a year earlier, meaning there’s no clear oil price imperative to adjust output quotas meaningfully. And even if some countries were to be assigned large new production ceilings during the audit, it’s unlikely OPEC+ will be pushing to release extra barrels onto the market. In the run-up to the meeting, Riyadh and Baghdad both said their output had recovered from wartime losses to levels that exceeded their agreed OPEC+ quotas. Before that, war-related disruption in Hormuz had forced Gulf nations to shutter output and rendered OPEC+ quotas something of a paper exercise. If the conflict flares anew, any quotas could once again become superfluous. But if the recent recovery in traffic endures, the numbers will become increasingly relevant. In addition to the uncertainties gripping the market, the audit will add an extra layer of complexity to Sunday’s decision-making process. On Nov. 16, officials from OPEC’s secretariat in Vienna and representatives from several countries held an online session to mark the conclusion of the DeGolyer and MacNaughton audit, and nations received their own results. These figures are to be used as the “baselines,” or starting points, for new production targets taking effect in January, though exactly how the new quotas will be calculated remains unclear, delegates said. They asked not to be identified as the process is private. One delegate said the Nov. 16 meeting was short and didn’t give members much opportunity to debate the new capacity levels. They said they were surprised that the group didn’t share a list of every country’s new capacity figures. OPEC’s secretariat in Vienna didn’t respond to a request for comment. Between April 2025 and September 2026, a subgroup of OPEC+ members has formally restored two layers of output halted in 2023 through a series of monthly quota increases, which continued even when the Iran war rendered the hikes symbolic. That process still technically leaves offline a third tranche of output that was idled back in 2022, though factoring this into new targets for 2027 is further complicated by the deterioration of output capacity many members have experienced in the meantime, owing to issues like under-investment and sanctions. In practice, the capacity review may ultimately allow only a handful of countries to boost production. Many members are already close to their limits, while others — most notably Saudi Arabia — are expected to retain spare capacity. The country that has most intensely lobbied for a higher baseline, and the right to pump more, is Iraq. In June, the nation’s oil ministry briefly warned it could decide “whether to remain in or withdraw” from the organization — founded in Baghdad more than six decades ago — if the results of its capacity assessment weren’t high enough. While the country subsequently withdrew the threat, Baghdad has chafed for years at OPEC quotas while it seeks to rebuild its shattered economy. Baghdad is seeking a production baseline of 6 million barrels a day, people familiar with the matter said in September. The warning carried extra weight because it came just weeks after the UAE announced its departure from the group after decades of stalwart membership, citing frustrations with limits on deploying supplies from new oil projects. Abu Dhabi’s production has subsequently reached new records of more than 5 million barrels a day, according to the IEA. Previous reviews of how much members can pump have proved contentious. An assessment of Angola’s capacity in 2023 spurred the country to quit OPEC after 16 years of membership. Ultimately, though, the fate of the war — rather than the outcome of the audit — may have the biggest influence of all on how much oil OPEC nations end up pumping in the coming year. Oil flows have held up in recent weeks, despite a surge in attacks by Iran on vessels going through Hormuz. At the same time, the US is maintaining a strict blockade on Iran’s shipping, pressuring Tehran. “Given Iran’s stated objective to break the blockade by any means necessary, the actual live fire in the region could still be more consequential in the near term than any rhetorical fireworks over production targets even with the recent rise in Hormuz transits,” said Helima Croft, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.body: Port Houston Shares Ship Channel Monthly Trade, Market Report Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 24, 2026 © Port Houston Trade activity across the Houston Ship Channel region continued to grow, reinforcing the waterway's role in supporting American industries, jobs, and economic activity. Foreign tonnage increased 15% year to date through September, reaching 200.2 million tons, driven by a 20% rise in exports. Deep draft vessel transits also increased 12% in October, reflecting continued maritime activity along the channel. The Houston Ship Channel region also continues to play a role in U.S. energy exports. Through September, Houston accounted for 32% of U.S. crude oil exports and nearly 65% of the year-to-date increase in oil exports nationwide. The Netherlands, Mexico, and Japan were the region's three leading export destinations during the same period, highlighting Houston's connections to global markets. Domestic cargo also accounts for a notable share of activity along the Houston Ship Channel. Based on monthly indicators and historical data published by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Port Houston estimates that 67.6 million short tons of domestic cargo moved through the region during the first nine months of 2026, up approximately 3.8% from the estimated 65.1 million short tons through September 2025. At Port Houston's public terminals, October brought multiple container milestones. Total container volume reached 415,326 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), up 14% year over year and the highest October volume on record. Loaded imports reached an all-time monthly high of 199,302 TEUs, surpassing the previous record set in May, while loaded exports climbed to 144,334 TEUs, also setting an October record. Through the first 10 months of 2026, Port Houston handled a record 3.76 million TEUs, up 4% from the same period last year. Growth extended beyond containers. Steel tonnage at the public terminals increased 74% to 504,010 tons year over year, while general cargo rose 170% to 217,633 tons. Shipments of steel, packaged cement, and other industrial materials support construction, manufacturing, and energy-related industries that contribute to the regional economy. Key Takeaways ﻿﻿Regional foreign trade: The Houston Ship Channel region handled 22.3 million tons of foreign cargo in September, up 13% year over year. Exports increased 16%, underscoring the region's role in connecting American industries to global markets. ﻿﻿Energy exports: Houston accounted for 32% of U.S. crude oil exports and nearly 65% of the year-to-date increase in national crude oil exports through September. ﻿﻿Vessel activity: October deep-draft vessel transits increased 12% compared to the same month last year. Year-to-date deep-draft traffic is up 8%, while barge transits have increased 7%. ﻿﻿Record-setting container activity: October marked a record month for total container volume and loaded exports, while loaded imports reached an all-time monthly high. Year-to-date container volume also reached a record 3.76 million TEUs through October, reflecting sustained cargo activity at Port Houston's public terminals. ﻿﻿Industrial cargo: Steel tonnage at the public terminals increased 74% in October, while general cargo rose 170%. Year-to-date general cargo volume is up 59%, reflecting increased movement of industrial and project cargo, including packaged cement. ﻿﻿What's moving: Through October, containerized imports increased across several major commodity categories, including apparel and accessories (+19%), machinery, appliances, and electronics (+12%), resins and plastics (+11%), and hardware and construction materials (+8%). Glaser, Pointe Coupee Parish, as secretary; and Johnny B. Bradberry, East Baton Rouge Parish as treasurer. Donald M. He is a partner and owner-operator of Schexnayder Planting and Manufacturing and serves as owner/operator of R. Schexnayder & Sons, LLC. Mr. Schenayder has long been active in agricultural advocacy and conservation leadership. He has served as president of the West Baton Rouge Farm Bureau Board since 2019 and as Louisiana Farm Bureau State Chairman of the Soybeans, Wheat and Feed Grain Committee for more than 15 years. He has also served for more than 25 years as a commissioner of the Upper Delta Soil and Water Conservation District and has been a board member of the Louisiana Landowners Association since 2020. In addition to his agricultural work, Mr. Schexnayder has played a significant role in regional economic development through his service on the Greater Baton Rouge Port Commission since 1998. Rev. Shelton C. Dixon , vice president, is the organizer and pastor of Greater Mount Olive Missionary Baptist Church in Baton Rouge, which he founded in 1996. He currently serves as General Secretary of the National Baptist Convention of America International, Inc. and since October 2019 has been serving as General President of the Louisiana Home and Foreign Missions Baptist Convention. Rev. Dixon was appointed to the Greater Baton Rouge Port Commission in 2020. His service to the community includes leadership roles with numerous civic and faith-based organizations. He also serves as a board member on the Louisiana Board of Embalmers and Funeral Directors. Ted H. Glaser , secretary, is a longtime Louisiana farmer and respected agricultural leader. He and his son, Abram, operate Glaser Farms Partnership in Pointe Coupee Parish, established in 1980, where they primarily produce sugarcane. Over the years, Mr. Glaser has held numerous leadership roles within the agricultural community, including serving as First Vice President of the Louisiana Farm Bureau and as a board member for Southern Farm Bureau Casualty Company and Farm Bureau Mutual Insurance Company. In recognition of his contributions to the industry, he was named Louisiana Farmer of the Year in 2000. His public service includes work with the USDA County Committee, Tri-Parish Cotton Gin, and the Louisiana Farm Bureau Marketing Board. He remains actively engaged in both his local community and the state through his service on the Louisiana Board of Regents and the Greater Baton Rouge Port Commission. Johnny B. Bradberry , treasurer, serves as President of G.E.C., Inc. (GEC), where he leads the engineering firm's strategic direction, operational performance, business development, and long-term growth initiatives. With more than 50 years of experience across engineering, public service, transportation, coastal restoration, oil and gas, and industrial development, he brings extensive leadership experience and a broad understanding of complex infrastructure and environmental challenges. Prior to joining GEC, Mr. Bradberry served as Executive Assistant to the Governor for Coastal Activities and Chairman of the Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority, helping guide implementation of Louisiana's Coastal Master Plan. He also served as Secretary of the Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development, overseeing statewide transportation programs and infrastructure investments. His career includes 28 years in the upstream and midstream oil and gas industry, as well as executive leadership roles with TOPCOR Companies and Volkert, Inc. He has served on the Port of Greater Baton Rouge Port Commission since 2024. articles.body: Containers Europe Maersk storms into megamax league Adis Ajdin November 25, 2026 0 591 1 minute read Maersk Maersk Danish liner giant AP Moller-Maersk has confirmed an order for 12 ultra-large containerships of 24,000 teu, marking its entry into the largest boxship segment with an investment estimated at around $2.9bn. The Copenhagen-based group said the dual-fuel vessels would be delivered in 2030 and 2031, becoming the biggest ships in its fleet. Each vessel will be equipped with engines capable of running on conventional marine fuel or LNG, with the 12-ship series adding 288,000 teu of nominal capacity. Maersk has declined to identify the shipbuilder or disclose the contract value. Shipbuilding sources have previously put the price of the vessels at around $240m apiece. The order follows weeks of negotiations with Chinese shipbuilders, with both Hengli Heavy Industries and Hudong-Zhonghua linked to the project. Earlier market reports pointed to a possible 12-ship contract with options for another dozen, although Maersk’s latest confirmation covers only the initial 12 vessels. The move represents a significant departure from the carrier’s previous preference for slightly smaller ships offering greater deployment flexibility. Its largest existing containerships, the second-generation Triple-E vessels, have capacity of around 20,500 teu. The latest deal adds to Maersk’s renewed appetite for newbuildings after years of comparatively restrained ordering. In September, the company confirmed contracts for 26 LNG dual-fuel ships of 18,600 teu (pictured), scheduled for delivery in 2029 and 2030. That followed an order for eight vessels of the same size at China’s New Times Shipbuilding in February. Including the latest megamax series, Maersk has now confirmed 46 containership newbuildings during 2026, representing a combined nominal capacity of more than 920,000 teu. The orders come against a backdrop of record contracting across the container sector, with the global newbuilding orderbook already exceeding 15m teu and further large-scale investments being pursued by the industry’s biggest carriers. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo Marine insurer The Swedish Club is warning shipowners against non-essential transits of the Strait of Hormuz as escalating attacks on commercial shipping, mounting congestion and persistent navigational interference further deteriorate the security environment in the Middle East. In an operational update issued Tuesday, the Gothenburg-based P&I club reaffirmed its recommendation that members avoid the strategic waterway unless passage is operationally essential. The warning follows a fresh wave of attacks on merchant vessels, particularly tankers navigating waters off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula. The warning comes as the International Maritime Organization (IMO) raised its tally of confirmed maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and wider Middle East to 141 as of November 23, with 25 seafarers confirmed dead. The latest additions include three vessels damaged off Oman between November 17 and 20. The actual scale of the crisis could be considerably greater. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) had already recorded 181 regional security incidents as of November 12, although the two organizations apply different reporting and verification criteria. Despite ongoing U.S.-facilitated transits, commercial shipping activity through Hormuz remains well below prewar levels. Independent monitoring cited by the Club recorded just 106 facilitated transits between November 15 and 18, averaging 26.5 vessels per day. The insurer also warned that ships accumulating at anchorages east of the Strait face heightened exposure to potential attacks, particularly during prolonged periods at anchor. The continuing U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and Tehran’s expanding blacklist of commercial vessels have introduced additional risks for shipowners. Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority reportedly increased its list of non-compliant vessels to 240 earlier this month. The Swedish Club urged operators to reassess their war-risk insurance arrangements, sanctions exposure, navigational capabilities and crew readiness before committing to voyages through the region. Crucially, the insurer cautioned that neither the continued movement of commercial shipping nor previous successful passages should be interpreted as assurances of safe transit. The advisory underscores the widening disconnect between efforts to restore commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and the security risks that merchant ships and their crews continue to face on a daily basis. articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Operations Grounded bulker pulled free off French coast Adis Ajdin November 25, 2026 0 2,432 1 minute read French Navy French Navy Salvors have successfully refloated the 28,200 dwt bulk carrier Miro G , four days after the ship was driven onto a beach on France’s Atlantic coast. The 2011-built, Malta-flagged bulker was pulled clear of the shoreline at Cap de l’Homy, near Lit-et-Mixe, on Tuesday afternoon by Les Abeilles International’s emergency response tug Abeille Bretagne. The vessel is set to be towed north to Le Verdon, at the mouth of the Gironde estuary, according to Landes prefect Gilles Clavreul, who confirmed that no pollution had been detected. The breakthrough followed days of preparations involving Dutch specialist SMIT Salvage, appointed by the shipowner, Les Abeilles International and experts from the French navy. Salvors took advantage of improving sea conditions and a rising tide, pumping ballast water out of the 169-m-long bulker to reduce its draught before pulling it free using a 1,900-m high-strength synthetic towline. Shallow waters had prevented the tug from approaching within about 900 m of the stranded vessel. As reported by Splash on Monday, the Miro G ran aground early on Friday after gusts of up to 48 knots caused it to drag its anchors. The ship was sailing in ballast towards Rouen. Nineteen of the vessel’s 22 crew were airlifted to safety on Friday, with the remaining three evacuated alongside salvage personnel on Saturday ahead of deteriorating weather. articles.title: Used Supertankers Now Cost More Than New Ships as Hormuz War Upends Shipping Markets
articles.summary: The war with Iran has so severely distorted the global oil tanker market that 15-year-old supertankers are now worth considerably more than brand-new vessels, highlighting the extraordinary premium placed on...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche The war with Iran has so severely distorted the global oil tanker market that 15-year-old supertankers are now worth considerably more than brand-new vessels, highlighting the extraordinary premium placed on immediately available shipping capacity. Belgian shipping group CMB.TECH revealed Tuesday in its third-quarter earnings report that the market value of a 15-year-old very large crude carrier (VLCC) has reached $165 million, some 25% above the $132 million price of ordering a new vessel, according to Clarksons data. The valuation is more than three-and-a-half times the 10-year average of $46 million for a tanker of that age. While newbuildings ordered today may take years to deliver, existing vessels can immediately capitalize on some of the highest tanker freight rates ever recorded. The unusual price inversion underscores how the war has fundamentally altered the economics of moving oil out of the Middle East. A Growing Capacity Crunch Although Middle Eastern oil exports have recovered substantially since the early months of the conflict, the shipping industry is relying on increasingly inefficient arrangements to move crude through the Strait of Hormuz. Combined oil exports from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Qatar reached 10.9 million barrels per day in October, up from 6.7 million barrels per day in April. However, much of that recovery has been facilitated by shuttle voyages and ship-to-ship transfers in the relatively safer waters of the Gulf of Oman. CMB.TECH estimates that 141 tankers are now dedicated exclusively to shuttling crude and petroleum products, with VLCCs accounting for 72% of those vessels. However, according to the CMB.TECH, the number of vessels deployed for shuttling only partly explains why tanker tonnage has become so tight. “A key additional factor is waiting time, with average round voyages extending to 23 days compared with an optimal 9 to 10 days,” the company said. The arrangement effectively removes significant tanker capacity from the wider international market, even as the global fleet continues to grow. The resulting shortage has spilled into other trading regions, driving up freight rates far beyond the Middle East as charterers compete for available tonnage. Unprecedented Earnings CMB.TECH’s Euronav tanker division reported average VLCC spot earnings of $149,945 per day in the third quarter, compared with $30,486 per day a year earlier. So far in the fourth quarter, those earnings have climbed to an extraordinary $635,199 per day, with 59% of available vessel days booked. The company’s Suezmax fleet is also benefiting, securing fourth-quarter spot earnings averaging $377,164 per day, with 68% of available days booked. The booming market has prompted CMB.TECH to capitalize on soaring vessel valuations. The company reported third-quarter net profit of $373.9 million, compared with $17.3 million a year earlier, including $100.2 million in gains from the sale of two Suezmax tankers. Three additional tanker sales are expected to generate approximately $190.8 million in gains during the fourth quarter. A Growing Risk of Reversal The extraordinary market conditions are also encouraging investment in new tanker capacity. The global VLCC orderbook now stands at 33.1% of the existing fleet, while the Suezmax orderbook has reached 29.3%, according to Clarksons data presented by CMB.TECH. An eventual normalization of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could release significant tanker capacity back into the international market, potentially coinciding with a wave of newbuilding deliveries in the coming years. Until then, however, CMB.TECH expects the availability of vessels, rather than underlying oil demand, to remain the primary driver of crude tanker earnings. For now, the fact that a 15-year-old supertanker commands a $33 million premium over a new vessel illustrates just how valuable existing shipping capacity has become in a world at war. articles.body: Rates & Surcharges Top Right Maersk introduces document amendment fee in North America November 24, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Maersk will introduce a Transport Document Amendment Fee for certain shipments loading from ports in the United States and Canada. The charge will take effect on 1 January 2027. A fee of US$75 will apply to eligible amendment requests submitted three or more calendar days after the containers have been loaded aboard the vessel at the first load port. Maersk refers to the new timeframe as the “Laden on Board + 3 Day Rule”. The fee will cover late changes to transport document details, including requests to change the document type from a negotiable Bill of Lading to a Sea Waybill or vice versa. Amendments excluded from the fee The charge will not apply to: Seal number additions or modifications Mandatory reference changes required for regulatory or compliance purposes House Bill of Lading requests, amendments or cancellations Out-of-gauge shipments Maersk noted that the fee may still apply when a single request combines an excluded amendment with other chargeable document changes. Customers submitting eligible requests through Maersk.com will be able to view the applicable fee, select the payer and payment terms, and accept the relevant conditions before completing the submission. articles.body: Business Developments & Projects November 24, 2026 · 1 minute ago African expansion on the cards for Eco Wave Power with potential 100 MW development Eco Wave Power is exploring a potential 100 MW wave energy initiative in Africa, following its South African feasibility study. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Eco Wave Power Israel-headquartered developer Eco Wave Power has set its sights on a potential expansion in Africa, after its U.S. subsidiary received a letter of intent (LOI) from an African electricity utility to explore up to 100 MW of wave energy capacity, building on its feasibility study in South Africa, which identified approximately 8.3 MW of potential wave energy capacity. Eco Wave Power’s U.S. subsidiary has received a letter of intent from an electricity utility in Africa regarding the proposed exploration and development of up to 100 MW of wave energy capacity. The LOI expresses interest in evaluating wave energy as a means of diversifying electricity sources, strengthening energy security and increasing renewable energy's contribution to the electricity supply. The company, which has not disclosed the utility's identity and the proposed project location at this stage, explains that the initiative represents a significant potential expansion of its activities in Africa, building on the firm's completed feasibility study for approximately 8.3 MW of potential wave energy capacity at South Africa's Port of Ngqura. Eco Wave Power and the undisclosed utility are now expected to advance discussions regarding a proposed feasibility study to assess suitable locations, wave resources, and generation potential, technical and environmental considerations, grid integration, commercial viability, preliminary capital and operating costs, opportunities for local workforce participation and a phased implementation roadmap. " This letter of intent represents an exciting opportunity to build on our progress in Africa and explore the potential for up to 100 MW of wave energy capacity. Our work at South Africa's Port of Ngqura provided valuable experience in evaluating how existing marine infrastructure could support wave energy generation. We now have an opportunity to apply that experience to a substantially larger proposed initiative. " — Inna Braverman Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Eco Wave Power The company emphasizes that the utility indicated its readiness to meet with the company’s U.S. subsidiary for further discussions regarding the proposed initiative. The potential scale of up to 100 MW reflects the duo's interest in evaluating a substantial wave energy opportunity. The proposed feasibility study would determine whether, where, and in what phases that capacity could be technically and commercially viable. Eco Wave Power's technology is designed to generate electricity from ocean and sea waves using floaters attached to coastal structures, with energy conversion equipment located onshore. The proposed assessment would examine opportunities to apply this approach at suitable sites. Eco Wave Power first entered the African market in July 2025 through an agreement with Africa Great Future Development Ltd. (AGFDL) to conduct a feasibility study for a potential wave energy project at the Port of Ngqura in South Africa. According to Eco Wave Power, the new LOI represents its second significant step into the African market and an opportunity to evaluate its technology at a substantially larger potential scale. We look forward to advancing discussions with the utility and defining a rigorous feasibility study to assess suitable sites, commercial potential and a phased path toward possible deployment. " — Braverman added. The firm points out that the initiative remains subject to completion of feasibility and technical assessments, agreement on project scope, and commercial terms, execution of definitive agreements, applicable regulatory and permitting approvals, and appropriate project financing. The LOI does not constitute a definitive agreement to construct or purchase a 100 MW project, and there can be no assurance that the initiative will proceed or reach the contemplated capacity. articles.title: Seatrium to cut Singapore workforce as it consolidates shipyards
articles.summary: Singapore-based marine engineering group Seatrium has announced plans to reduce approximately 2% of its Singapore workforce as part of a restructuring programme aimed at improving operational efficiency and aligning resources with future projects. The announcement, made on 24 November 2026, marks the company’s first...
articles.body: Singapore-based marine engineering group Seatrium has announced plans to reduce approximately 2% of its Singapore workforce as part of a restructuring programme aimed at improving operational efficiency and aligning resources with future projects. The announcement, made on 24 November 2026, marks the company’s first workforce restructuring exercise since its merger in 2023. The programme will also accelerate the consolidation of Seatrium’s shipyard operations in Singapore and support a more integrated global operating model. Seatrium said its worldwide yard network has already been reduced from 15 facilities in 2023 to 11. Singapore shipyards to undergo further changes Under the restructuring, Tuas Boulevard Yard will remain Seatrium’s flagship mega-yard, while Admiralty Yard will continue to be scaled down ahead of its planned return to the Singapore Government in 2028. The group’s other Singapore facilities, Benoi Yard, Pioneer Yard and Tuas Yard, will focus more closely on projects that best match their operational capabilities. In particular, Tuas Yard will shift towards higher-value vessel repairs and upgrades. These changes form part of the One Seatrium Global Delivery Model, which coordinates the company’s international shipyard network from Singapore. The model is intended to improve capacity utilisation and allow projects to be assigned to the most suitable facilities. Workforce reduction follows operational review Seatrium said it reviewed redeployment opportunities, employee training and other workforce measures before deciding to eliminate certain positions. Approximately 2% of its Singapore workforce will be affected by the restructuring. “Our people have been instrumental in building Seatrium into the global business it is today, and we are deeply grateful for every colleague’s contributions over the past 60 years,” said Chris Ong, Chief Executive Officer of Seatrium. “We are not downsizing or simply cost cutting. We are repositioning and readying Seatrium to capture new opportunities,” Ong added. The company said it invested approximately S$7 million in employee training during 2025 and delivered more than 600,000 training hours globally. Seatrium Employees Union (SEU) was informed of the restructuring in advance and has worked with the company to support affected employees. The union said the assistance would include outplacement support and access to employment services through Singapore’s labour movement. Seatrium expects the restructuring to proceed without disruption to ongoing operations or project execution. The company has not disclosed the exact number of affected employees or the financial savings expected from the programme.

ExxonMobil and the Block 15 partners have formalized a final investment decision estimated at $4 billion for the redevelopment of Kizomba A , Kizomba B , and the development of the Likembe field , concluding the FID of the Block 15 Life Extension project , following the approval of the Kizomba C redevelopment in 2025, according to Angola’s National Agency of Petroleum, Gas and Biofuels (ANPG) . articles.body: Containers Europe Danaos bags $611m in fresh boxship charters Adis Ajdin November 24, 2026 0 498 1 minute read Danaos Danaos Greek containership owner Danaos has secured another $611m in contracted revenue through a string of new fixtures and charter extensions, taking its forward revenue backlog to $5bn. The John Coustas-led company revealed the deals in its latest quarterly update, with a comparison of its fleet employment schedules showing fresh contracts for six containership newbuildings alongside longer employment for several ships already on the water. Four 5,300 teu vessels ordered at CSSC’s Huangpu Wenchong Shipyard earlier this year have secured three-year charters. The quartet, scheduled for delivery in 2028 and 2029, was previously listed without employment. Another two 9,000 teu newbuildings booked in September for delivery in early 2029 have secured charters running for at least 4.8 years. Danaos has also extended employment coverage for three of its largest containerships, the 2012-built, 13,100 teu Kota Plumbago, Kota Primrose and Kota Peony , from 2027 into 2029. The latest fixtures leave just two of the New York-listed owner’s 28 containership newbuildings without disclosed charter commitments. Both are 1,800 teu feeders scheduled for delivery in 2028 and 2029. Danaos has now covered 94% of its available containership operating days for next year, 84% for 2028 and 71% for 2029. More than half of its 2030 capacity is also contracted. The company previously disclosed $683m in additional charter revenue in August. Meanwhile, Danaos has formally confirmed it is putting plans for a separate Norwegian listing of its dry bulk business on hold, a move previously reported by Splash in October. The AThens-based owner controls 78 containerships totalling more than 502,000 teu, alongside 11 capesizes. Its newbuilding programme includes 28 boxships and four 211,000 dwt newcastlemax bulkers. articles.body: ShipVet Appoints New CEO as Founder Steps Back Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 24, 2026 James Stairmand (Credit: ShipVet) Marine assurance and vessel vetting company ShipVet has appointed James Stairmand as chief executive officer, effective November 2026, as founder Captain Fintan Cullen moves to a non-executive role. Stairmand, previously the company's chief commercial officer, joined ShipVet as part of a management buy-in in late 2024, backed by Frontier Development Capital. Since the investment, ShipVet has expanded its vessel vetting team with specialists from major oil companies, rebuilt its digital platform and strengthened its sanctions screening capabilities. The company's platform supports vessel assessments and sanctions screening, with maritime specialists evaluating the findings against clients' vetting policies and providing recommendations. Stairmand has more than 20 years of experience in the commodities sector and previously founded, expanded and exited OnlineFuels, a digital marketplace for downstream fuels. Cullen, who founded ShipVet in 1997, will remain involved with the company as a non-executive director. Headquartered in London, ShipVet provides independent vessel vetting and marine assurance services to the oil, gas and commodities sectors, including vessel suitability assessments, vetting policy design and sanctions screening. “Charterers need to understand the risks associated with a vessel and how those risks relate to their own requirements. Our job is to provide a clear assessment and be available to discuss it. “Fintan has built a business that clients trust. Since the buy-in, we have invested in the expertise and technology needed to develop that service further. My focus as CEO is to bring it to more charterers while preserving the judgement and responsiveness that have underpinned ShipVet’s work,” said James Stairmand, Chief Executive Officer of ShipVet.

articles.title: Port of Gothenburg invests in electrified rail access
articles.summary: The Port of Gothenburg is installing overhead line infrastructure on the container terminal’s handling tracks, allowing electric locomotives to run directly to and from the terminal. This removes the need for diesel locomotives or detours via the port departure yard, and is intended to raise capacity, cut emissions...
articles.body: The Port of Gothenburg is installing overhead line infrastructure on the container terminal’s handling tracks, allowing electric locomotives to run directly to and from the terminal. This removes the need for diesel locomotives or detours via the port departure yard, and is intended to raise capacity, cut emissions and make rail operations more efficient. Construction is due to begin next year. The terminal is operated by APM Terminals and handles about 80 trains a week, linking the port with more than 20 destinations across Sweden. Rail freight is growing: a record 529,000 TEU moved to and from the port by rail last year, and volumes have continued to rise in 2026. The project aims to make better use of existing infrastructure as demand increases. The investment is expected to shorten total turnaround times for container rail shuttles by up to 30 minutes, because trains can depart straight from the terminal rather than spending time in the departure yard. It will also improve handling of trains of up to 750 metres, whereas train length is currently limited by the 630-metre tracks in the departure yard. The scope includes about 1,250 metres of overhead line, 38 line masts with foundations, upgraded level crossing protection systems and a new emergency access road, improving safety and resilience for both road and rail traffic. Birna Ödefors, Managing Director of APM Terminals Gothenburg, said that electrifying the final stretch removes another fossil fuel dependency from the transport flow, giving customers better opportunities to cut emissions and strengthening rail as a sustainable and competitive option. Robert Sommar, Railway Manager at the Port of Gothenburg, said more efficient traffic arrangements will create better conditions for both growth and sustainable transport.

articles.body: Europe Offshore EnEarth takes control of Scottish carbon storage project Bojan Lepic November 24, 2026 0 276 1 minute read EnEarth EnEarth Carbon storage developer EnEarth has agreed to acquire Storegga’s 30% stake in the Acorn carbon capture and storage project in northeast Scotland, taking over as lead developer of the North Sea scheme. The acquisition is expected to be completed before the end of 2026, subject to the necessary approvals. Financial terms have not been disclosed. The project includes the Acorn and East Mey offshore storage areas, which have estimated combined storage capacity exceeding 140m tonnes of CO2. EnEarth, which was established by Greek oil and gas producer Energean, is also developing the Prinos CO2 storage project in Greece and pursuing carbon storage opportunities elsewhere in southeastern Europe. The acquisition follows Storegga’s decision last year to review its business and seek a buyer for its Acorn interest. The project has faced uncertainty over funding and the pace of UK government support, with a final investment decision still outstanding. EnEarth aims to progress the development towards commercial sanction, with potential operations beginning in the early 2030s. U.S. Coast Guard Photo The U.S. Coast Guard has sought a specialized salvage inspection of the damaged No. 2 diesel generator aboard USCGC Healy , seeking to identify components that can be reclaimed and reused following a catastrophic engine failure. The procurement goes well beyond a conventional engine repair contract. The Coast Guard’s October 21 statement of work calls for a comprehensive, component-by-component assessment of the damaged Sulzer 12ZAV40S engine, including measurements against allowable clearances, an evaluation of component wear and identification of parts suitable for reclamation and reuse. The contractor must document its findings in a comprehensive report with high-resolution color photographs. The Coast Guard announced its intent to award the work on a sole-source basis to Virginia-based Defense Maritime Solutions. The inspection was scheduled for October 26–30 at Coast Guard Base Seattle. The solicitation also included an optional work item, capped at $100,000, to inspect, repair and requalify the engine’s camshaft. The documents do not establish whether that option was exercised or what the inspection ultimately found. The work follows the July casualty, when Healy suffered a catastrophic overspeed failure of its No. 2 main propulsion diesel generator while operating northwest of Port Angeles, Washington. The vessel was towed to Seattle on July 13. Related procurement documents describe a fire in Generator Room No. 2 that exposed fire-detection equipment and wiring to high temperatures, causing a ground fault and requiring extensive replacement work. The casualty disrupted the cutter’s planned Arctic summer deployment . The Coast Guard has also been addressing maintenance requirements on engines No. 1 and No. 3. A separate October procurement sought overhaul of their governors and overspeed protection equipment. Both governors had accumulated more than 40,000 operating hours, with no documented service or overhaul history. The work also called for replacing a damaged cylinder head on engine No. 3. The removed head and dummy valve were to be sent to a machine shop for inspection and reconditioning in accordance with original equipment manufacturer specifications. The Coast Guard specified cylinder head part number 107.122.903.200, National Stock Number 2815-01-465-2075. Separately, supply-chain database records for the part list no active suppliers and indicate that the government does not hold the technical-data rights needed to have alternative manufacturers reproduce it using the proprietary data. The database’s acquisition guidance calls for purchasing directly from the actual manufacturer. This does not establish that the part is unavailable, but it could limit alternative sourcing options if the original manufacturer cannot supply it . “Most of the machinery systems aboard are antiquated and for some there aren’t even parts,” Vice Commandant of the Coast Guard Admiral Kevin E. Lunday said previously following a fire aboard Healy in 2024. Engine challenges are not entirely new for Healy . In 2020, a fire damaged the ship’s starboard propulsion motor, forcing it to abandon an Arctic deployment . The Coast Guard replaced the motor with a spare that had been stored at the Coast Guard Yard in Baltimore for 23 years. Moving the roughly 100-ton unit to a California shipyard required a barge voyage through the Panama Canal and removal of part of the ship’s hull for installation. The latest procurement records do not establish whether the No. 2 diesel generator can be returned to service or which of its components can be recovered. They do, however, show the Coast Guard undertaking a detailed salvage assessment and highlight potential parts-sourcing challenges across the remaining propulsion plant. KYIV, Nov 24 (Reuters) – Ukraine’s foreign minister said on Tuesday a drone attack against a Russian military vessel and cargo ship in Libyan waters at the weekend was a legitimate act of self-defense, following criticism from the government in Tripoli. Andrii Sybiha said that both Russian naval vessels and cargo ships transporting military equipment were valid targets and Ukraine’s right to self-defense was enshrined in the United Nations charter, Article 51. Libya’s Tripoli-based Government of National Unity condemned on Monday the Ukrainian military operation that sank the Russian naval corvette Merkury in the eastern port of Benghazi. It said Libya would not accept being drawn into the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Benghazi is controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army has ties with Russia. The internationally recognized Government of National Unity in Tripoli controls western Libya. “Ukraine is not ‘dragging’ anyone into the war or ‘transferring’ the war anywhere,” Sybiha said on the Telegram messaging app. “Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasize that Ukraine’s actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people.” International law does not limit the right to self-defense to the territory where the aggression takes place: it can be on the territory of the aggressor, or in international waters, Sybiha said. Russia, he said, was the one endangering third countries by using their civilian infrastructure for its military purposes. The Institute for the Study of War said the Russian naval corvette had stopped over for several days at Benghazi port to refuel and resupply, under a cooperation agreement, as it escorted cargo ships that can carry military supplies to Russia. The eastern government in Benghazi on Monday said there were indications the naval drones were launched from western Libya and asked the UN to investigate allegations that Ukraine has deployed military experts there. Russia’s defense minister has not commented publicly on the attack. In an interview published on Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy confirmed that Ukraine was responsible for a separate drone strike on Saturday on a Russian cargo vessel in the international waters of the Gulf of Finland. He said the vessel, Sparta II, was a legitimate target because it was carrying weapons. The damaged vessel was towed back to the Russian port of St Petersburg, Russia’s Transport Ministry said on Tuesday. articles.title: Torvald Klaveness puts $7bn price tag on shipping inefficiencies
articles.summary: Norwegian shipping group Torvald Klaveness has identified around $7bn in potential annual savings across dry bulk and product tanker shipping, with excessive transaction costs, underutilised vessels and poor port coordination among the industry’s biggest sources of inefficiency. The Oslo-based company’s new study,...
articles.body: Bunkering Dry Cargo Operations Ports and Logistics Tankers Torvald Klaveness puts $7bn price tag on shipping inefficiencies Adis Ajdin November 24, 2026 0 571 2 minutes read Torvald Klaveness Torvald Klaveness Norwegian shipping group Torvald Klaveness has identified around $7bn in potential annual savings across dry bulk and product tanker shipping, with excessive transaction costs, underutilised vessels and poor port coordination among the industry’s biggest sources of inefficiency. The Oslo-based company’s new study, examining approximately $190bn in annual freight spending across the two sectors, suggests the wider opportunity could be worth between $10bn and $20bn a year. The research examined around 50 potential sources of inefficiency, with 14 investigated in detail using voyage data, market benchmarks and operational evidence. At the top of the list is an estimated $1.6bn in avoidable transaction costs, reflecting commercial arrangements where charges are linked to freight and time-charter values rather than improvements in efficiency. Another $1.4bn could be unlocked by deploying larger vessels on trades currently served by smaller ships, while better use of available cargo capacity represents a further $1bn opportunity. Port inefficiencies also feature prominently. Klaveness calculates that around $700m could potentially be saved by improving vessel arrival times, reducing the practice of ships steaming at higher speeds only to wait at anchor for a berth. The study examined approximately 429,000 dry bulk port calls during 2025, identifying around 16,000 cases involving vessels that had sailed for at least seven days before spending three or more days waiting. The wider utilisation figures are equally revealing. Capesize bulkers spent just 40% of their on-hire days sailing laden during 2025, compared with 33% in ballast and another 12% waiting in port. Klaveness also identified around $400m in potential fuel savings from addressing misaligned incentives in time-charter contracts, where shipowners may have limited financial motivation to invest in efficiency improvements because charterers pay for the fuel. Other costs include an estimated $300m from claims and disputes, while unreliable shipping schedules could be adding between $300m and $700m annually to the financing costs of excess inventories held by dry bulk importers. The study, conducted over nearly four months with independent adviser Cardo Partners, draws on Klaveness’s internal voyage database alongside external market data. It puts annual freight spending at approximately $140bn for dry bulk and $50bn for product tankers, with the identified inefficiencies spanning commercial contracting, vessel deployment, port operations and cargo owners’ working capital. Ernst Meyer, chief executive of Torvald Klaveness, argued that the problem lies less with individual companies than with the way shipping’s commercial interests are structured. “Every party is acting rationally, but the incentives don’t line up,” Meyer said. Klaveness noted that better coordination between cargo owners, charterers, operators, shipowners and ports, supported by improved data and artificial intelligence, could unlock much of the value currently being lost. The group has already been pursuing trading efficiency through its dry bulk operations, combination carriers and digital business, including tools designed to improve cargo planning and commercial decisions. Klaveness cautioned that the $7bn figure represents an indicative sum of potential savings rather than a net savings forecast, with some overlap between individual estimates. A further $3bn in opportunities has been identified but not yet quantified, while the broader $10bn to $20bn range includes potential savings that remain unexplored. articles.body: Asia Europe Offshore Indonesia clears offshore gas development for Eni-Petronas venture Bojan Lepic November 24, 2026 0 778 1 minute read Eni Eni Indonesian authorities have approved the development plan for the Geliga gas field offshore East Kalimantan, paving the way for a major new deepwater production hub involving an FPSO vessel and 15 subsea wells. The approval, announced by Italian energy major Eni, covers the integrated development of Geliga and neighbouring Gula in the Kutei Basin, containing an estimated 8.1 trillion cubic feet of gas in place. Geliga, discovered earlier this year, holds approximately 5.9 tcf of gas and 250m barrels of associated condensate in place, while Gula contains another 2.2 tcf of gas. Searah, the joint venture established in June by Eni and Malaysia’s Petronas, will operate the project. The development calls for 15 subsea wells connected to a newbuild FPSO capable of processing around 1bn cubic feet of gas and 80,000 barrels of condensate per day, with storage capacity of approximately 1.4m barrels. Peak production is expected to reach 1bn cubic feet of gas and 50,000 barrels of condensate per day. Gas will be exported through the Santan Terminal and East Kalimantan pipeline network, supplying domestic customers and the Bontang LNG plant. According to Indonesian regulator SKK Migas, the development plan was approved just six months after Geliga’s discovery, with first production targeted for 2029. The project will become the third major gas production hub in the Kutei Basin, alongside the producing South Hub and the North Hub development sanctioned in March. The North Hub involves 16 subsea wells tied to another newbuild FPSO and is expected to start production in 2028. Eni recently brought the Maha gas field onstream, connecting two subsea wells to the existing Jangkrik floating production unit. With the three hubs, Eni expects gross production in East Kalimantan to reach about 3bn cubic feet of gas and 140,000 barrels of condensate per day by the end of the decade. No FPSO construction or subsea installation contracts have been announced for Geliga/Gula, which has yet to reach a final investment decision. articles.body: Europe Operations One Maritime Generation targets specialist shipmanagement niche Sam Chambers November 24, 2026 0 471 1 minute read Two German shipping professionals from markedly different maritime backgrounds have established a shipmanagement company in Hamburg, targeting a niche in the market for vessels engaged in complex and unconventional operations. One Maritime Generation brings together Gerda Rohden, a veteran of German family-owned shipping, and Anna-Maria Renken, a qualified lawyer whose maritime career spans commercial shipping, offshore operations, ocean racing and humanitarian search-and-rescue missions. Registered in Hamburg, the company is looking to build a business providing third-party shipmanagement services, with vessels operated by non-governmental organisations (NGOs) among its target markets. Rohden comes from a shipping family whose shipmanagement activities date back to 1959. She has spent more than two decades running the family business, overseeing a diversified fleet encompassing bulk carriers, containerships, general cargo ships and offshore vessels. She was also previously involved in the management of Liberty Blue Shipmanagement. Renken brings more than a decade of international maritime experience, combining legal expertise with practical knowledge of vessel acquisitions, technical management, flag state requirements and classification. The new venture’s services encompass technical and operational management, procurement, financial reporting, insurance, regulatory compliance and crewing support. The company is placing particular emphasis on developing a “no-blame culture”, encouraging employees to identify and address operational shortcomings without fear of repercussions. Its focus on humanitarian and other specialist vessels differentiates the business from many established third-party shipmanagers, with such operations often presenting unusual regulatory, insurance and crewing challenges that require expertise extending beyond conventional merchant shipping.Moreover, in a segment of shipping where men are almost exclusively picked for the top roles, the founders gender sets this new venture apart.
